— AI_POLICY.md:
# AI Contribution Policy

— AI_POLICY.md:
This policy sets clear expectations for AI-assisted contributions. It is not
an anti-AI stance — maintainers and contributors alike use AI tools in their
daily workflows, and we encourage you to do the same. AI can accelerate
learning, improve documentation, generate test scaffolding, and help explore
design alternatives. We welcome contributors who use AI as a productivity
amplifier, not as a substitute for understanding.

— AI_POLICY.md:
**AI tools are welcome in the Chainloop contributor workflow. The human
contributor is always accountable for every line submitted.**

— AI_POLICY.md:
- **Own your changes.** You must be able to explain every change you submit.
  "The AI generated it" is never an acceptable answer during review.
- **Design before coding.** For non-trivial changes, open a GitHub Issue with
  clear reasoning before a PR. PRs that ignore established patterns will be
  closed.
- **Quality over quantity.** One well-understood, well-tested PR is worth more
  than many AI-assisted drive-by fixes. A flood of low-effort PRs exhausts
  maintainer attention and delays everyone in the queue.
- **Tests are required.** Bug fixes need regression tests; new features need
  unit and integration tests. AI-generated tests that do not actually exercise
  the relevant behaviour will be rejected.
- **Legal compliance.** Chainloop is [Apache 2.0 licensed](LICENSE).
  Contribut

— AI_POLICY.md:
If AI assisted in producing any part of your contribution, disclose it in the
PR description. Add an `Assisted-by:` trailer to each affected commit:

— AI_POLICY.md:
```
Assisted-by: GitHub Copilot
Assisted-by: Claude Code
Assisted-by: ChatGPT o3
Assisted-by: OpenCode
```

— AI_POLICY.md:
Use the name of the AI coding tool that actually produced the work (e.g.
`OpenCode`, `Claude Code`, `GitHub Copilot`), not the underlying model. Do not
blindly copy an example — pick the value that matches the tool you are running.

— AI_POLICY.md:
- **Respond personally.** Do not pipe review feedback back into an AI and
  apply the output blindly. Responses during review must reflect genuine
  understanding of the code and the project's design goals.
- **No AI ping-pong.** If maintainers observe a pattern of AI-driven responses
  without real engagement, the PR will be closed without further explanation.
- Maintainers reserve the right to close any low-effort AI contribution without
  a detailed technical critique.

— AI_POLICY.md:

— AI_POLICY.md:
Maintainers also use AI tools: for reviewing changes, exploring implementation
options, and improving documentation. The same disclosure and ownership
expectations apply to maintainer-authored commits.

- **LLM traffic is replayed, not live.** A package with `testdata/*.httprr`
  replays through `internal/httprr` with no flags and no credentials. Each of
  those files is an **HTTP recording**: one request-and-response exchange,
  captured once against a real model and replayed on every run afterwards, so
  tests stay deterministic and need no API key. `session/vertexai` uses a
  second, unrelated system for **RPC recordings** — `rpcreplay` with

  live model or network call to a test.
- `-httprecord` takes a **regexp matched against the recording's file path**,
  not a `-run` test-name filter. Keep it as narrow as the set of recordings you
  mean to replace: recording against a live model produces a different resp

issues.title: First build without zstd leaves Deferred empty: the newest-first publish takes the skipped list, so run two still rewrites the index
issues.body:
Follow-on from #5108. On a first build of 400+ sessions, the newest-first partial publish (`publishNewestFirst`, internal/index/ingest.go:1653) commits through `commitManifest` and `mergeIngestDiag`, which folds and clears the list of rollouts skipped for want of zstd. The full build then commits `Deferred` empty.

Stand: 4000 plain + 1500 `.zst` Codex rollouts, no zstd on PATH. After the first build the manifest has `files=4000 deferred=0`, so the second run still rewrites the index; only the third is fresh. Nothing is lost.

Expected: `Deferred` holds the 1500 rollouts after the first build. Folding without clearing in the partial publish, or reading the list once per pass, would do it.
issues.triage_reason: publishNewestFirst (internal/index/ingest.go) lets mergeIngestDiag/DiagSnapshot drain diagZstdMissing in internal/sources/diag.go; saving and restoring the no-zstd set around writeSessions, as is done for emptied/collisions/merged, is a small fix. Some judgement is needed on the other diag maps and on the test setup.
issues.summary: publishNewestFirst's manifest write drained the zstd-skipped path list, so the full build committed Deferred empty. It now saves the list before the partial write and restores it afterwards via new sources.DiagRestoreNoZstd; added a unit test for the helper.
issues.pr_title: fix(index): keep Deferred zstd list across newest-first publish
issues.pr_body:
Fixes #5110

## Summary

On a first build of a large corpus, `publishNewestFirst` writes a partial manifest. That write drained the list of rollouts skipped for want of zstd, so the full build committed `Deferred` empty. The second run then rewrote the index again.

`publishNewestFirst` now saves the list before the partial write and puts it back afterwards with the new `sources.DiagRestoreNoZstd`. The full build folds the list as before.

## Test plan

- Added `TestFirstBuildKeepsDeferredAcrossNewestFirstPublish` in `internal/index`. It builds enough plain rollouts to trigger the partial publish, plus one `.zst` rollout with no zstd available, and checks that the manifest `Deferred` holds the compressed rollout after the first build.
- Added `TestDiagRestoreNoZstd` in `internal/sources` for the new helper.
- The regression test and the project's checks pass.

## Notes

No data was lost before this change. The only effect was an extra index rewrite on the second run.

The test asserts Deferred holds the .zst path and fails with 0 entries.

issues.title: Light theme on 256-colour terminals: key chips vanish into their panel (surf and surf2 both xterm 254)
issues.body:
On a terminal without truecolor (no `COLORTERM`, e.g. macOS Terminal.app) the light palette's surfaces round onto the same xterm-256 entries:

```
base   #eff1f5 -> 255    mantle #e6e9ef -> 255
surf   #e4e6ee -> 254    surf2  #dce0e8 -> 254
```

surf2 is the key-chip and button background (cmd/deja/tui_style.go), drawn on surf panels, so in light mode the chips lose their fill. Found by the 256-colour check added with #5102, which only pins surfaces against the background. Expected: surf2 lands one step darker, like the dark palette's 235/236/237/239.
issues.triage_reason: Change the light palette's surf2 hex in cmd/deja/tui_style.go to one that rounds to a different xterm-256 entry than surf (254), and extend TestThemeSurfacesStayApartIn256Colours in tui_more_test.go to check surf vs surf2.
issues.skip_reason: rejected by human: fixed upstream by maintainer in #5342
issues.summary: Light palette surf2 (key chip/button bg) was #dce0e8, rounding to the same xterm-256 entry (254) as surf. Changed it to #d8dce5 so it gets its own entry; the regression test and cmd/deja package tests pass.
issues.pr_title: fix(tui): give light theme key chips their own 256-colour shade
issues.pr_body:
Fixes #5107

## Summary

On terminals without truecolor, the light palette's `surf` (#e4e6ee) and `surf2` (#dce0e8) both round to xterm 254. Key chips and buttons use `surf2` on `surf` panels, so the chips lose their fill.

This changes light `surf2` to #d8dce5, which gets its own xterm-256 entry, one step darker than `surf`.

## Test plan

issues.title: Rules Claude Code saved in its auto-memory never reach Codex, opencode or any other agent in the same project
issues.body:
Claude Code keeps an auto-memory per project (`~/.claude/projects/<encoded path>/memory/*.md`) and loads it at every session start. No other agent reads it, and deja doesn't either, so a rule the user taught Claude in a project is unknown to the Codex or opencode session started in the same directory.

Repro on a stand: a Claude memory file for `/tmp/tuip/payments` with the description `Retries in payments use internal/retry.Backoff; a hand-rolled sleep loop is rejected in review (zebra-quartz-17)`, then a Codex-style SessionStart:

```
$ echo '{"session_id":"probe-c1","cwd":"/tmp/tuip/payments","hook_event_name":"SessionStart","source":"startup"}' | deja hook-context | grep -c zebra-quartz-17
0
```

Control: the same file is what Claude Code itself loads, so the token is in Claude's context and in no other agent's.

On a real store with 48 memory files in one project, 0 of them reach a non-Claude session. The only project-level rules any agent gets from deja are promoted notes, and there was 1.

Expected: non-Claude sessions get the memory's descriptions (rules first, small budget), Claude doesn't get them twice, and the person can see and veto what is handed on.

issues.title: a page for adding memory to TRAE CLI
issues.body:
deja reads TRAE CLI and has `deja install trae` and `trae-auto`, but there is no `docs/guide/memory-for-trae.html`. 36 agents have one.

From `docs/registry/trae.md`: the store and its overrides (`TRAE_HOME`, `TRAECLI_HOME`, `DEJA_TRAE_ROOT`), resume with `traex resume <id>`, `deja install trae` adds the MCP server to `${TRAE_HOME:-~/.trae}/traecli.toml`, and `trae-auto` adds Codex's hooks to `hooks.json`, which TRAE runs once they are trusted at start-up. The page should say that last part plainly, since a hook that is never trusted never fires.

`docs/guide/memory-for-qwen.html` or `memory-for-kimi.html` is the template: what the agent forgets, one install line, what the hooks add, where the history lives.

Needs: an entry in the per-agent group of `scripts/gennav/main.go` and a `go run ./scripts/gennav` (the per-agent count on every page moves with it), sitemap rows in `docs/sitemap.xml` and `docs/sitemap.txt`, and a line in `docs/llms.txt`. `TestEveryGuidePageListsEveryPerAgentGuide` and `TestAPerAgentPageCountsTheOtherAgentsCorrectly` check the list and the "the other N agents" wording. Verify the install against a real `traex` before writing it down.

issues.title: a guide page for deleting Junie session history
issues.body:
JetBrains' Junie (the CLI, and the agent inside AI Assistant) has no delete-history page.

From `docs/registry/junie.md`:

- Each session is a directory, `${JUNIE_HOME:-~/.junie}/sessions/<session-id>/`, holding `events.jsonl`, `state.json`, `transcript.md` and one `task-*` directory per task.
- `sessions/index.jsonl` has a line per session with its `projectDir` and `taskName`.
- The home is `.junie` under the JVM's `user.home`, not `$HOME`, which matters on a machine where the two differ.

Worth saying on the page: removing the directory leaves the session's line in `index.jsonl`, and `transcript.md` is a second copy of the conversation.

`docs/guide/delete-kimi-code-session-history.html` is the closest template (directory per session plus an index).

Needs: an entry in `scripts/gennav/main.go` and a `go run ./scripts/gennav`, rows in `docs/sitemap.xml` and `docs/sitemap.txt`, a canonical link, a line in `docs/llms.txt`. The three guide tests named on the other delete-page issues will say what is missing. Check every path against a real install before writing it down.

issues.title: tests, recap and secrets suggest --limit 0, and their help never says what 0 does
issues.body:
When rows are cut, `deja tests`, `deja recap` and `deja secrets` each print a footer pointing at `--limit 0` for the rest (`cmd/deja/tests.go:202`, `recap.go:218`, `secrets.go:192`). Their help pages say `--limit n` and nothing about the default or about 0:

```
$ deja help tests
Usage:
  deja tests [--limit n] [--json]

Your build and test runs, week by week. Then the tests that failed on more
than one day.
```

`deja help recap` and `deja help secrets` read the same way. `docs/guide/commands.html` does say it ("--limit (8 tests by default, 0 for all)"), so the CLI is the only place it is missing. friction is different on purpose: it refuses 0, so leave it.

Done: the help entries at `cmd/deja/help_commands.go:121`, `:126` and `:151` say the default and that 0 shows all, with the same numbers commands.html uses (8 tests, 12 sessions, 10 sessions).

Test: a table test in `cmd/deja/help_commands_test.go` (or beside the other help tests) that `deja help <cmd>` for each of the three contains `0` near `--limit`.

issues.title: deja help names six --role values; deja last --help names summary too
issues.body:
`deja --role summary <query>` works (`knownRoles`, `cmd/deja/main.go:2547`), and `deja help last` lists it. The search-flag block in `deja help` does not, and it writes `tool-output` as the prose `(tool output)`:

```
$ deja help | grep -A1 -- --role
  --role <name>          only turns from one role: user, assistant, tool
                         (tool output), files, command, edit
$ deja help last | sed -n 2p
  deja last [n] [--json] [--project name] [--harness name] [--from machine|local] [--since duration] [--role user|assistant|tool|files|command|edit|summary]
$ deja --role summary parseConfig
deja: "parseConfig" matched nothing under role "summary"
deja: this index holds no summary records at all — the harnesses it read do not write them, or wrote none yet
```

The rows are at `cmd/deja/help_commands.go:342-343`. Add `summary`, and keep the line inside the help column width (the next row wraps the same way).

Test: `TestHelpNamesEveryRoleThatMatches` in `cmd/deja/help_role_values_test.go` loops over files, command and edit; add `sources.RoleSummary` to that list for the flag block.

issues.title: deja check - extra says check needs '-'
issues.body:
Given the argument it asks for plus one more, `deja check` reports the argument as missing. `deja completion` does the same:

```
$ deja check - extra
deja: check needs '-' to read a plan from stdin
$ deja completion bash extra
deja: completion needs bash, zsh, fish, or powershell
```

Both checks are `len(args) != 1 || ...` with one message for every failure: `cmd/deja/check.go:25-26` and `cmd/deja/completion.go:13-14`. Split them so a second argument gets its own message, e.g. `check takes only '-', got an extra "extra"` and `completion takes one shell, got "bash" and "extra"`. No argument and a wrong argument keep today's wording.

Test: `TestRunCheckRequiresDash` in `cmd/deja/check_test.go` already passes `{"-", "extra"}` and checks only that it errors; assert the error names `extra`. Add the same for `captureRun(t, "completion", "bash", "extra")` in `cmd/deja/main_test.go`.

issues.title: share and restore drop a second argument without a word
issues.body:
`deja share` and `deja restore` each take one argument. A second one is ignored:

```
$ deja share 01a0 extra
# deja share: 01a0c3e4-1111-4222-8333-444455556666

- Project: tmp/proj
$ deja restore main.go config.go
No replaced spans recorded for "main.go"
```

The restore case is the confusing one: someone who meant `config.go` is told nothing exists, and `config.go` has a span:

```
$ deja restore config.go
1 replaced span recorded for config.go
```

Control: `deja blame config.go extra` says `deja: blame accepts one path`, and `deja show 01a0 extra` says `deja: show accepts one session id`.

`cmd/deja/share.go:37` reads `args[0]` and never looks at the rest. `cmd/deja/restore.go:81-83` keeps the first path and skips the others. Refuse a second positional in both, before the index is opened.

Test: extend `TestShareRefusesFlagsItCannotHonour` in `cmd/deja/share_test.go` with `share <id> extra`, and `TestRestoreUnknownPathAndBadArgs` in `cmd/deja/restore_test.go` with two paths. Both must return an error naming the extra argument.
issues.triage_reason: Add a second-positional refusal in cmd/deja/share.go (before findByPrefix) and in the default branch of the arg loop in cmd/deja/restore.go, mirroring the existing blame/show messages; extend TestShareRefusesFlagsItCannotHonour and TestRestoreUnknownPathAndBadArgs.
issues.summary: share and restore now refuse a second positional argument with an error naming it, before the index is opened.
issues.pr_title: fix(cli): refuse a second argument in share and restore
issues.pr_body:
## Summary

Fixes #5076

`deja share <id> extra` and `deja restore a.go b.go` used to ignore the extra argument. `restore` looked only at the first path, so a user who meant the second path was told nothing was recorded for the first.

Both commands now return an error that names the extra argument, for example `share accepts one session id, got extra argument "extra"`. This matches `blame` and `show`. The check runs before the index is opened.

## Test plan

- Extended `TestShareRefusesFlagsItCannotHonour` with `share loc extra`. It expects an error that names `extra`.
- Extended `TestRestoreUnknownPathAndBadArgs` with `restore a.go b.go`. It expects an error that names `b.go`.
- The existing tests and project checks pass.

## Notes

Only a second positional argument is affected. Flag handling and single-argument use are unchanged.

issues.pr_text:
fix(cli): refuse a second argument in share and restore

## Summary

Fixes #5076

`deja share <id> extra` and `deja restore a.go b.go` used to ignore the extra argument. `restore` looked only at the first path, so a user who meant the second path was told nothing was recorded for the first.

Both commands now return an error that names the extra argument, for example `share accepts one session id, got extra argument "extra"`. This matches `blame` and `show`. The check runs before the index is opened.

## Test plan

- Extended `TestShareRefusesFlagsItCannotHonour` with `share loc extra`. It expects an error that names `extra`.
- Extended `TestRestoreUnknownPathAndBadArgs` with `restore a.go b.go`. It expects an error that names `b.go`.
- The existing tests and project checks pass.

## Notes

Only a second positional argument is affected. Flag handling and single-argument use are unchanged.

I ran into a command that quietly ignores part of what I typed. I think it should say so, as `blame` and `show` already do.

issues.title: deja log 2 1 prints one entry: the second count wins without a word
issues.body:
`deja log` takes one count. Given two, it keeps the last and says nothing:

```
$ deja log 2 1
2026-10-16 10:38  search         0 B  (empty result)

showing 1 of 18 — `deja log 18` shows the rest
```

Control: `deja last` refuses the same input.

```
$ deja last 2 3
deja: last takes one count, got 2 and "3"
```

The loop at `cmd/deja/log.go:33-48` overwrites `n` on every number. Remember that a count was seen and refuse a second one with the same shape of message `last` uses. `--last` prints one digest and ignores a count; leave that alone, it is out of scope here.

Test: in `cmd/deja/log_test.go`, `runLogTo(&b, dir, []string{"2", "1"})` returns an error naming both numbers, and `[]string{"2"}` still works.

issues.title: --quiet completes where deja refuses it, and not where it works
issues.body:
`--quiet` belongs to `deja index` (`cmd/deja/main.go:558`). bash and zsh offer it to search too, and search refuses it. fish and PowerShell do the opposite: they leave it off `index`.

```
$ deja search foo --q<Tab>
--quiet
$ deja parseConfig --quiet
deja: search: unknown flag "--quiet" — `deja search --help` lists its flags; put it after `--` to search for the text
```

and on the index side:

```
$ deja completion fish | grep 'from index'
complete -c deja -n '__fish_seen_subcommand_from index' -l rebuild
$ deja completion powershell | grep "'index'"
            'index' { @('--rebuild', '-rebuild') }
```

Control: bash `deja index --q<Tab>` offers `--quiet`, and `deja index --quiet` works.

In `cmd/deja/completion.go`: drop `--quiet` from the bash search lists at `:68` and `:204` and the zsh default at `:351`; add `-l quiet` for index in fish next to `:406`, and `'--quiet', '-quiet'` to the PowerShell index case at `:512`.

Test: extend `cmd/deja/completion_lists_test.go` (or add a dispatch test) so `deja search foo --` does not offer `--quiet` in any shell and `deja index --` offers it in all four.

issues.title: update --force completes in no shell
issues.body:
`deja update --force` writes over a binary a package manager owns (`deja help update`). `update` sits in the no-argument list in every completion script, so Tab offers nothing:

```
$ deja update --<Tab>

$ deja update --re
deja: update takes no arguments except --force, got "--re"
```

`for s in bash zsh fish powershell; do deja completion $s | grep update | grep -c force; done` prints `0` four times.

Take `update` out of the no-argument list in `cmd/deja/completion.go` (bash `:197`, zsh `:348`, PowerShell `:554`) and give it a case offering `--force` in all four shells. The zsh and fish description can repeat the help: it writes over a binary a package manager owns.

Test: `cmd/deja/completion_update_dispatch_test.go`: `deja update --` offers `--force`.

issues.title: Tab offers wip and brief twelve flags, and both refuse every one
issues.body:
`deja wip` takes `--json` only. `deja brief` takes no arguments. Both fall through to the default case in every completion script but fish, so Tab offers the search flags:

```
$ deja wip --<Tab>
--json --re --all --no-embed --harness --project --since --role --session --rebuild --quiet --limit
$ deja wip --re
deja: wip takes --json and nothing else
$ deja brief --<Tab>
--json --re --all --no-embed --harness --project --since --role --session --rebuild --quiet --limit
$ deja brief --json
deja: brief takes no arguments — got "--json"
```

In `cmd/deja/completion.go`, add `brief` to the no-argument list (bash `:197`, zsh `:348`, PowerShell `:554`) and give `wip` its own case offering `--json` in all four shells.

Test: `cmd/deja/completion_wip_dispatch_test.go`: `deja wip --` offers `--json` and not `--re`, and `deja brief --` offers neither.

issues.title: log --last and view --no-open complete in no shell
issues.body:
`deja log` takes a count, `--last` and `--json` (`logFlags`, `cmd/deja/main.go:3208`). `deja view` takes `--out path` and `--no-open` (`viewFlags`, `:3207`). Neither has a completion case:

```
$ deja log --<Tab>
--json --re --all --no-embed --harness --project --since --role --session --rebuild --quiet --limit
$ deja log --re
deja: log: unknown flag "--re" — `deja log --help` lists its flags
$ deja view --<Tab>
--json --re --all --no-embed --harness --project --since --role --session --rebuild --quiet --limit
$ deja view --re
deja: view: unknown flag "--re" — `deja view --help` lists its flags
```

Add a `log` case (`--last --json`) and a `view` case (`--out --no-open`, files after `--out`) to the four scripts in `cmd/deja/completion.go`: bash before `:197`, zsh before `:348`, fish beside the subcommand lines, PowerShell before `:554`.

Test: `cmd/deja/completion_log_view_dispatch_test.go`: `deja log --` offers `--last`, `deja view --` offers `--no-open`, and neither offers `--re`.

issues.title: recap --since completes nowhere, and Tab offers recap flags it refuses
issues.body:
`deja recap` takes `--since`, `--limit` and `--json` (`cmd/deja/recap.go:62-89`). There is no completion case, so Tab offers the search list:

```
$ deja recap --<Tab>
--json --re --all --no-embed --harness --project --since --role --session --rebuild --quiet --limit
$ deja recap --project proj
deja: recap: unknown flag "--project" — it takes --since 7d, --limit n and --json
```

`--since` is in the list only because search has it too, and fish offers nothing.

Add a `recap` case offering `--since --limit --json` to each script in `cmd/deja/completion.go` (bash before `:197`, zsh before `:348`, fish beside the subcommand lines, PowerShell before `:554`). In zsh and fish the `--since` description can say it takes a duration like `30d` (the default is 7d).

Test: `cmd/deja/completion_recap_dispatch_test.go`: `deja recap --` offers `--since`, `--limit`, `--json` and not `--project` or `--re`.

issues.title: fix, friction and tests complete twelve flags and take two
issues.body:
`deja fix`, `deja friction` and `deja tests` each take `--limit n` and `--json` and nothing else. None has a completion case, so Tab offers the search flags, and ten of the twelve are refused:

```
$ deja tests --<Tab>
--json --re --all --no-embed --harness --project --since --role --session --rebuild --quiet --limit
$ deja tests --since 7d
deja: tests: unknown flag "--since" — it takes --limit n and --json
$ deja friction --re
deja: friction: unknown flag "--re" — it takes --limit n and --json
$ deja fix parseConfig --project proj
deja: fix: unknown flag "--project" — `deja fix --help` lists its flags
```

fish offers nothing for any of the three.

Add a `fix|friction|tests` case offering `--limit --json` to the four scripts in `cmd/deja/completion.go` (bash before `:197`, zsh before `:348`, fish beside the subcommand lines, PowerShell before `:554`). After `--limit`, offer nothing.

Test: `cmd/deja/completion_limit_json_dispatch_test.go` with `checkCompletionDispatch`: for each of the three, `deja <cmd> --` offers `--limit` and `--json` and does not offer `--since` or `--re`.
issues.triage_reason: Add a `fix|friction|tests` case offering --limit/--json to the four scripts in cmd/deja/completion.go, plus a new completion_limit_json_dispatch_test.go using the existing checkCompletionDispatch helper (same pattern as the neighbouring *_dispatch_test.go files). Small and well specified. Only risk is matching each shell's syntax and the 'nothing after --limit' behaviour.
issues.feedback:
Attempt 1:
Reviewer rejected:
- The issue says to offer nothing after `--limit`. The fish line `complete -c deja -n '__fish_seen_subcommand_from fix friction tests' -l limit -r -d 'Max results'` uses `-r` without `-f`, so fish still offers file completions after `--limit`. Use `-x` instead, as the `restore --span` line already does, so no candidates are offered. Bash, zsh and PowerShell do return nothing there.
issues.summary: Added fix|friction|tests completion cases offering --limit and --json to bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell scripts; fish --limit now uses -x so no candidates (including files) are offered after it. Regression test passes.
issues.pr_title: fix(completion): offer only --limit and --json for fix, friction, tests
issues.pr_body:

`deja fix`, `deja friction` and `deja tests` accept only `--limit n` and `--json`. They had no completion case, so Tab offered the search flags, and most of those are refused. fish offered nothing.

## Test plan

For each of `fix`, `friction` and `tests`, `deja <cmd> --` must offer `--limit` and `--json` and must not offer `--since` or `--re`. The test and the project checks pass.

## Notes

No change to flag parsing. Only the completion scripts changed.

Fixes #5068

## Summary

`deja fix`, `deja friction` and `deja tests` accept only `--limit n` and `--json`. They had no completion case, so Tab offered the search flags, and most of those are refused. fish offered nothing.

This adds a `fix|friction|tests` case to the bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell scripts in `cmd/deja/completion.go`. Each offers `--limit` and `--json`. After `--limit`, nothing is offered. In fish, `--limit` uses `-x`, so files are not offered after it either.

## Test plan

Added `TestLimitJSONCompletionDispatch` in `cmd/deja/completion_limit_json_dispatch_test.go`. It uses `checkCompletionDispatch`. issues.title: files and how complete search flags they refuse, and never --all-projects
issues.body:
`deja files` and `deja how` take the same four flags: `--project`, `--all-projects`, `--limit`, `--json`. Neither has a completion case, so Tab offers the twelve search flags. Two of them work by accident (`--project`, `--limit`), the rest are refused, and `--all-projects`, the one each help page points at, is never offered.

```
$ deja files parseConfig --<Tab>
--json --re --all --no-embed --harness --project --since --role --session --rebuild --quiet --limit
$ deja files parseConfig --harness claude
deja: files: unknown flag "--harness" — `deja files --help` lists its flags
$ deja how go --since 7d
deja: how: unknown flag "--since"; a query that starts with a dash goes after `--`
$ deja how go --all-projects
$ go test ./...
  ran once in 1 session · last Oct 14
```

zsh gives the same list. fish has no `files` or `how` line at all (`grep -c "subcommand_from files'"` on `deja completion fish` is 0).

Add one shared case for `files|how` to each script in `cmd/deja/completion.go` (bash before `:197`, zsh before `:348`, fish beside the subcommand lines, PowerShell before `:554`) offering `--project --all-projects --limit --json`.

Test: `cmd/deja/completion_files_dispatch_test.go` using `checkCompletionDispatch`: `deja files x --` and `deja how x --` both offer `--all-projects` and `--limit`, and neither offers `--harness` or `--re`.

issues.title: promote --state, --note, --tag and --to complete in no shell
issues.body:
`deja promote` takes `--state`, `--note`, `--tag` and `--to` (`promoteFlags` at `cmd/deja/main.go:3211`). No completion script has a `promote` case, so bash, zsh and PowerShell fall through to the search flags and fish offers nothing. In bash:

```

--json --re --all --no-embed --harness --project --since --role --session --rebuild --quiet --limit
$ deja promote 01a0 --state <Tab>
--json --re --all --no-embed --harness --project --since --role --session --rebuild --quiet --limit
$ deja promote 01a0 --re
deja: promote: unknown flag "--re" — did you mean --to?
```

Every flag Tab offers is refused, and the four `--state` values (`accepted rejected superseded stale`) are never offered.

Add a `promote` case to all four scripts in `cmd/deja/completion.go`: bash before the no-argument list at `:197`, zsh before `:348`, fish beside the other subcommand lines, PowerShell before `:554`. After `--state`, offer the four states. After `--to`, complete files. After `--note` and `--tag`, offer nothing.

issues.title: Semantic tier: key vectors by content so they survive index rewrites, and let vectors retrieve on their own
issues.body:
Follow-up to #4975. Two observations from running `deja embed` (0.21.7/0.22.0, Ollama `embeddinggemma-2:270m`) on a ~112k-record store of Claude Code, Codex and omp sessions.

### 1. The sidecar rarely survives until the next `deja embed`

The checkpoint stores the generation taken when the run started. If any update rewrites `records.bin` before the next `deja embed` (a torn last line, a Claude tail with a failed `tool_result` - `claudeExitResumes`, a removed file), `sameLayout` fails at `internal/embed/sidecar.go:113` and all vectors are discarded, so the resume from #4568 does not apply and the next run re-embeds everything (~45 min here). On a machine with the prompt hook installed that happened within 18 minutes of a finished run: sidecar generation `11:42:22Z+69005616`, index `12:00:15Z+69241197`. Search then refuses the sidecar as stale until the next embed (the notice from #2208 is there now; the refusal itself remains).

It cannot be fixed inside `EmbedIndex` as written: after a rewrite the old `records.bin` is gone and each vector holds only `Offset` and `Key`, so there is nothing to map it back by.

**Proposal:** sidecar v2 stores per vector `(Key, record Time, 64-bit hash of the text)`. `EmbedIndex` replaces the `sameLayout` check with a lookup by that triple over the current records: matches are carried over with their new offset, only new or changed records are embedded. `SemanticSearch` already reads every record (`semantic.go:39`), so it can resolve by the same triple instead of `byOffset` and drop the hard `Stale` refusal. The rerank uses only `Key` (`rerank.go:43-51`), so the `Stale` check in `maybeRerank` (`cmd/deja/embed.go:125`) could already be dropped today; new sessions simply have no cosine until the next embed.

### 2. A vector leg that retrieves on its own

Today vectors only rerank the top 64 lexical hits, or run when lexical finds nothing (`cmd/deja/embed.go:153`). On 20 real queries against a fresh sidecar (10 Russian, 10 English; one relevant session each, so treat the numbers as direction only):

| mode | hit@5 | MRR |
|---|---|---|
| lexical (`--no-embed`) | 6 | 0.26 |
| lexical + rerank (current) | 6 | 0.30 |
| best cosine per session, query with the model's prefix (`task: search result \| query: `) | 15 | 0.40 |

The gap is mostly cross-language and paraphrase: a Russian question about a session held in English shares no tokens with it (lexical 2/10 in the top 5, vector 7/10). Two things would capture that: a vector-first leg ranking sessions by best cosine (fused with lexical, or as a `--semantic` mode), and per-model query/document prefixes (EmbeddingGemma and nomic both expect them; raw queries scored 10/20 vs 15/20 prefixed).

agentsview and qmd key their vectors by message UUID / content hash for the reason in (1).

issues.title: Support storing code review results in S3-compatible storage
issues.body:
### Problem Statement

Currently, `ocr review` stores all review results (including session data and artifacts) in the local directory `~/.open-code-review`. This approach has limitations in Kubernetes environments:

- Data gets lost when the pod is restarted or rescheduled.
- `ocr viewer` cannot reliably access historical review sessions across pod lifecycles.
- No built-in support for durable, shared, or versioned storage of review artifacts.

### Proposed Solution

Introduce native support for using **S3-compatible object storage** to persist review results:

1. Allow configuring an S3 bucket as the storage backend for review data via config file or CLI flags (e.g., `--storage-type s3`, `--s3-bucket`, `--s3-endpoint`, etc.).
2. Store all review session metadata, diffs, comments, and generated artifacts in the specified S3 bucket.
3. Ensure `ocr viewer` can read review sessions directly from S3 (either via same config or explicit parameters).
4. Keep the local `~/.open-code-review` directory optional (e.g., only for temporary caching or CLI configuration).

### Example config snippet
```yaml
storage:
  type: s3
  s3:
    endpoint: https://s3.mycompany.internal
    bucket: ocr-review-results
    region: us-west-2
    access_key_id: ${OCR_S3_ACCESS_KEY}
    secret_access_key: ${OCR_S3_SECRET_KEY}
    path_prefix: prod/
```

### Alternatives Considered

_No response_

### Affected Area

CLI / Commands

### Additional Context

### Benefits
- Long-term persistence and durability of review data.
- Shared access across teams and CI pipelines.
- Easy backup, versioning, and compliance using S3 features.
issues.triage_reason: Large cross-cutting feature: it needs a storage abstraction over local session/artifact I/O, an S3 client that requires go.mod/go.sum changes (paths the bot may not edit), new config and flags, and viewer changes, plus maintainer design decisions.

issues.title: Proposal: ChatGPT-plan reviews in GitHub Actions through a user-run token broker
issues.body:
### Problem Statement

The ChatGPT sign-in added in #1622 works for local reviews, but the GitHub Action cannot use it today.

Refresh tokens rotate. Each refresh invalidates the previous refresh token, so a token kept in a GitHub secret goes stale after its first refresh, and sending a stale one ends the session until the user signs in again in a browser. Repository secrets are read when a run is queued, a workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot write secrets, and the secrets API has no conditional write. A rotating token in GitHub secrets breaks easily even with careful serialization.

OpenAI's Sign in with ChatGPT terms also say persistent token storage must be local and under the user's control, and that another user's activity must not trigger requests to the authenticated user's account. Storing the refresh token in GitHub, or using one person's sign-in for everyone's PRs, conflicts with both.

`action.yml` has no `chatgpt` path either. It runs `ocr config unset provider` and requires the API-key inputs.

### Proposed Solution

A small broker that runs on the user's own machine and is the only place the refresh token lives.

1. The user runs `ocr auth login --provider chatgpt` on their machine as today, then starts `ocr-chatgpt-broker`, a Go binary in this module that reuses `internal/chatgptauth` for refresh, ID-token verification, pending-refresh recovery and the locked store.
2. The workflow joins the user's Tailscale network as an ephemeral tagged node, so the broker needs no public port. `tailscale serve` provides HTTPS on its `*.ts.net` name.
3. The job requests a GitHub OIDC token and sends it to the broker. The broker verifies the signature and checks `repository_id`, `workflow_ref`, `event_name`, a broker-specific `aud`, and that `actor_id` equals the broker owner's GitHub ID.
4. The broker refreshes when needed, one refresh at a time, and returns an access-only credential valid for up to an hour. The runner never sees the refresh token and writes nothing back.
5. The action imports the access-only credential and runs the review with the `chatgpt` provider. Code goes from the runner to OpenAI the same way it does in a local review.

For a shared repository, a registry file on the default branch, protected by CODEOWNERS, maps approved GitHub user IDs to broker URLs and audiences. The workflow routes by `github.actor`, the person whose activity triggered the run. Users without a registered broker are skipped or fall back to the API-key route. The registry only routes. Each broker refuses any request whose `actor_id` is not its owner, so a wrong entry cannot spend another person's plan, and per-broker audiences stop a misrouted OIDC token from being replayed to a different broker.

OCR changes, by size:

- `OCR_CHATGPT_STORE_DIR` to set the credential store path. Small.
- An access-only credential mode that never refreshes, plus `ocr auth import`, `ocr auth refresh` and `ocr auth status --json`. A few hundred lines with tests.
- Detach the refresh request from caller cancellation. `oauth.go` sends the refresh POST with the caller's context, so a cancel or timeout after OpenAI has rotated the token can lose the new token and end the session. This affects local use too. Small.
- The broker binary with GitHub OIDC verification and a policy file. Around 500 lines plus tests.
- A `chatgpt` mode in `action.yml` that joins Tailscale, fetches from the broker and skips the API-key configuration. Around 150 lines.

All of it can be tested offline against the existing fake issuer fixtures.

### Alternatives Considered

- **Environment secret with write-back.** A serialized job refreshes, a GitHub App writes the new credential back, and a revision variable detects stale copies. Works for one repository per sign-in, but keeps the refresh token in GitHub and needs an App with Environments write access.
- **External store with compare-and-swap** (DynamoDB, S3 `If-Match`, Vault KV v2) reached through OIDC. Correct, but puts the refresh token on runners and needs cloud setup.
- **Broker proxies inference** instead of handing out access tokens. Every OpenAI request then comes from the user's machine, and long reviews refresh without a hook. The cost is a streaming proxy, and in a multi-user setup a misrouted request would send code to the wrong broker. I would keep this as a later option.
- **Self-hosted runner on the user's machine.** Simplest technically, but ties CI capacity to that machine.
- **Actions cache or artifacts.** Not usable. Cache entries are immutable and readable by PR authors, and artifacts are readable by anyone with repository access.

### Affected Area

CLI / Commands, Configuration, Other (GitHub Action)

### Additional Context

- Per-user setup: a Tailscale tag and OAuth client, the broker as a launchd or systemd service, two repository secrets, and the workflow. A later `ocr broker setup` command could shorten this.
- For upstream OCR I see this as an opt-in for maintainers. API keys would stay the default for the public Action and contributor PRs.
- Questions that need a live session: the usual `earliest_refresh_at` offset, whether reusing a rotated refresh token revokes the whole grant, and whether the 30-day refresh lifetime resets on each rotation.
- I will probably run this locally for my own projects either way.

@Qiyuanqiii what do you think? Would this be viable for OCR, or would you rather keep the Action on API keys and leave this outside the project?

issues.title: review hangs on stalled LLM request: bypasses --timeout and OCR_LLM_TIMEOUT, no retries, no session record
issues.body:
## Summary

`ocr review` intermittently hangs indefinitely at ~0% CPU on a stalled LLM request. Neither the group budget (`--timeout <minutes>`) nor the per-request HTTP timeout (`OCR_LLM_TIMEOUT`, default 300s) fires. No retry is attempted, no session row is recorded, and no partial output file is written. The only recovery is killing the process.

## Environment

- ocr v1.12.13 (fabbdb29) darwin/arm64, macOS 27
- Provider: openrouter (`z-ai/glm-5.3`), key in env — `ocr llm test` round-trips in ~4s while the wedge is happening
- Range review: `ocr review --from main --to HEAD --format json --output <file> --audience agent -b "<context>"`

## Repro evidence (single session, same 4-file/62-line diff)

| Run | Result |
|---|---|
| Run 1 | ✅ complete in 2m10s — 5 findings |
| Run 2 | ✅ complete in 46s — 3 findings |
| Run 3 | ❌ hung ~4 min, killed (no session, no output) |
| Run 4 | ❌ hung 16 min at 0.0% CPU (measured via ps), killed — 300s `OCR_LLM_TIMEOUT` and group budget never fired |
| Run 5 | ❌ hung with `--timeout 10` set, killed by external 420s watchdog — same stall |

Run 5 command (also had `--timeout 10`):

```
timeout 420 ocr review --from main --to HEAD --timeout 10 --format json --output /tmp/out.json --audience agent -b "…"
```

Additional observations:

- The hung runs never record a session row in `ocr session list` — the stall is early-phase, before session creation.
- `ocr llm test` succeeds normally immediately after killing a wedged run → provider/network healthy; the stall is in ocr's HTTP client path.
- Earlier the same evening, a different (322K-token) review failed as `error_class: timeout`, `failure_phase: context`, status 200, `duration_to_headers_ms: 1173` — i.e. a request that got 200 headers then stalled on body — which looks like the same class of stall, but in that path it at least produced a failure record. The wedge cases produce nothing.

## Diagnosis (from outside)

Pattern fits a stalled-but-open socket (e.g. server sends 200 headers, then silence) that the client's timeout stack doesn't cover — undici/fetch header timeouts often don't fire on already-established sockets. The retry report for the partial run showed `retried_requests: 0`, so the stall also bypasses the retry layer.

## Expected

- A stalled request is aborted at `OCR_LLM_TIMEOUT` seconds and retried.
- If it can't be recovered, the run records a session/manifest and exits non-zero instead of hanging forever.

Happy to provide more instrumentation (node debug logs, tcpdump of the stalled request) if useful.
issues.triage_reason: The hang is not reproducible from the report and the diagnosis assumes a Node/undici stack. internal/llm already tests per-request timeouts for stalled headers and bodies, so the real stall location is unknown and needs maintainer investigation.

issues.title: Let more than one reviewer share the comment poster on a PR
issues.body:
### Problem Statement

We run several automated reviewers on the same pull request: OCR itself, plus a security scan and two other model reviewers. All of them post as `github-actions[bot]` with the workflow token. We'd like all of them to post through OCR's `post-review-comments.js`, because its inline review, line-resolution fallback, sticky summary and outdated-thread resolution are exactly what we want.

The poster's identity is hard-coded to `ocr`, though: the per-comment marker, the summary marker and the ownership check all assume it. So when two callers post on one PR:

- each treats the other's threads as its own, and `resolve_outdated` closes them;
- incremental dedupe drops a finding because another reviewer has a comment on the same lines;
- the sticky summaries overwrite each other;
- every summary reads "OpenCodeReview".

### Proposed Solution

A `namespace` option on `runPostReviewComments` (default `ocr`, so OCR's own output is byte-identical). It parameterizes every marker the poster writes and every pattern it matches, so each namespace owns its own threads, dedupe history and sticky summary. A `displayName` option (default `OpenCodeReview`) renames the summaries.

Separately, and only if you'd find them useful:

1. A post-only composite sub-action (`post/action.yml`) that runs the poster on a result file another tool produced, with no LLM or install steps.
2. An opt-in `resolve_on_empty_result`. Today the resolver runs only after a run that produced findings, so a clean round after fixes never resolves its outdated threads. Opting in allows resolution after a well-formed `comments: []`, but never after unparseable output.

We have these working in a fork, with tests, and would open them as separate PRs: namespace and displayName first.

### Alternatives Considered

- **A second poster of our own.** That duplicates the batching, 422 line-resolution fallback and summary logic, and it still collides with OCR's threads, because both post as the same bot.
- **A different token per reviewer.** That needs a GitHub App per reviewer, which is heavy for a CI-only setup.

### Affected Area

Output / Formatting; Other (GitHub Action)

### Additional Context

Fork branch: https://github.com/studiomgmt/open-code-review/tree/feat/poster-namespace

AI disclosure: the analysis and the fork's code were produced with Claude Code (Anthropic Claude models). I have reviewed the changes and will answer review questions myself.

issues.title: WebUI: start a review from "ocr viewer" and stream its progress live (opt-in, loopback-only)
issues.body:
### Problem Statement

`ocr viewer` can browse and compare past review sessions, but it is read-only. To start a review you still need a terminal: `cd` into the repository, remember the flags for the diff range, and pass `--provider` / `--model` if you want a model other than the configured default. Then you switch to the browser to read the result.

For people who already live in the viewer (or who are less comfortable with the CLI), it would be useful to do the whole loop in one place:

1. choose a local repository,
2. choose the diff range and the model,
3. start the review and watch its progress live,
4. land on the finished session page that the viewer already renders.


### Proposed Solution


## 1. User-facing behaviour

- New opt-in flag: `ocr viewer --allow-run`. Without it the viewer behaves **exactly as today** (read-only, no new routes registered).
- A **New review** page with a form:
  - **Repository path**: absolute path to a local git work tree.
  - **Mode**: workspace changes, range (`--from` / `--to`), or single commit (`--commit`).
  - **Provider and model**: a dropdown filled from the built-in provider/model list (`llm.ListProviders()`), plus a free-text model field. It defaults to the configured provider and model.
  - Optional: background text (`--background`), effort (`--effort`), token budget (`--max-tokens-budget`).
- After **Start**, a live log view streams progress over **Server-Sent Events (SSE)**, with a **Cancel** button.
- When the run finishes, the page links to the existing session page `/r/{repo}/{sessionID}` (the `session_id` is taken from the JSON result).

## 2. Architecture

**Each run is a child process of the same binary.** The viewer starts `os.Executable()` with `review ... --format json --audience human`:

- `stderr` (human progress) is read line by line and forwarded as SSE `log` events.
- `stdout` (a single JSON document) is parsed at exit and sent as a final `result` event.

Why a child process instead of calling `internal/agent` in-process:

- Progress goes through the process-global writer in `internal/stdout`, and `stdout.Quiet()` is documented as main-goroutine-only. Two concurrent in-process runs could not keep their output apart.
- The CLI already has interrupt handling (`interrupt.go`) and process-group setup (`procattr_*.go`). Cancellation reuses both: SIGINT to the process group first, then a kill after a grace period.
- A panic or a hung run cannot take the viewer down.
- Sessions are persisted to `~/.opencodereview/sessions/` by the child exactly as a CLI run would, so the existing viewer pages work unchanged.

**Job manager** (new, inside `internal/viewer`):

- In-memory jobs with states `queued → running → succeeded | failed | cancelled`.
- A bounded log buffer per job (for example 5,000 lines / 2 MB). A browser that reconnects replays the log from `Last-Event-ID`.
- Finished jobs are evicted after a TTL. All child processes are killed when the viewer exits.

**Routes** (registered only with `--allow-run`):

| Method | Path | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/run` | New-review form |
| GET | `/api/models` | Provider names, model ids, which one is configured. **No secrets.** |
| POST | `/api/runs` | Validate input, start a job, return `202 {"id": ...}` |
| GET | `/api/runs/{id}/events` | SSE stream: `log`, `status`, `result` |
| POST | `/api/runs/{id}/cancel` | Cancel a running job |

SSE rather than WebSocket: the stream is one-way, SSE works with plain `net/http` with no new dependency, and the browser reconnects on its own.

## 3. Security

Starting a review spends API tokens and runs `git` against arbitrary local paths, so the run feature needs a stricter model than the read-only viewer.

**3.1 Off by default and loopback only**
- The run routes exist only with `--allow-run`.
- `--allow-run` **refuses to start** if `--addr` binds a non-loopback address (for example `:3000`) or if `OCR_VIEWER_ALLOWED_HOSTS` is set. There is no auth layer suited to a network, so the feature is not offered there.

**3.2 Per-launch secret token (similar to Jupyter)**
- At startup the viewer generates 32 random bytes (`crypto/rand`) and prints the URL as `http://localhost:5483/?token=...`.
- The first request exchanges the token for an `HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookie and redirects to the same URL without the token, so the token does not stay in the address bar or history.
- Every `/run` and `/api/*` request requires the cookie. The comparison is constant-time.
- This protects against other local users or processes on a shared machine, and together with the existing host guard it covers DNS rebinding.

**3.3 CSRF**
- State-changing routes are `POST` only.
- They require an `Origin` header equal to the viewer's own origin; a missing `Origin` is rejected.
- They require `Content-Type: application/json`, which forces a CORS preflight from any other site. The viewer sends no CORS headers, so the preflight fails.
- The `SameSite=Strict` cookie from 3.2 adds another layer.

**3.4 Input validation (no shell, no free-form arguments)**
- argv is built from a typed struct and run with `exec.Command`. There is **no shell** and no pass-through field for arbitrary flags.
- **Repository path**: must be absolute. It is cleaned with `filepath.Clean` and resolved with `filepath.EvalSymlinks`, must be a directory, and must equal `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`. An optional repeatable `--allow-run-root <dir>` restricts runs to repositories under given directories.
- **Refs** (`from` / `to` / `commit`): reject anything starting with `-` (git option injection), limit the charset and length, and check with `git rev-parse --verify` before starting.
- **Provider** must be a known provider. **Model** is limited to `[A-Za-z0-9._:/@-]` with a maximum length.
- Request bodies are capped with `http.MaxBytesReader` (for example 64 KB), and the background text has its own length limit.
- Phase 1 does **not** accept `--rule`, `--tools`, `--background-file` or `-o`, because those read or write arbitrary files. The run uses the repository's own `.opencodereview/` config, as the CLI does.

**3.5 Secrets stay in the CLI**
- No route reads or writes config. API keys are never sent to the browser or accepted from it.
- `/api/models` returns only names and a "configured" flag.
- The child inherits the viewer's environment, which is the same thing that happens when a user runs `ocr review` in a terminal.

**3.6 Resource limits**
- A maximum number of concurrent jobs (default 1) and at most one running job per repository.
- The existing `--timeout` applies. The form pre-fills a default `--max-tokens-budget` so a mistaken click does not start an unbounded run.
- Log buffers are bounded, and job records expire after the TTL.

**3.7 Rendering untrusted output**
- Log lines contain model output and source code, so they are treated as untrusted.
- They are sent as JSON-encoded SSE data. ANSI escapes are stripped on the server, and the client renders them only with `textContent`, never `innerHTML`.
- The current CSP (`script-src 'self'`, `form-action 'none'`, no `unsafe-inline`) stays **unchanged**. All new JS lives in `internal/viewer/static/`.

**3.8 Audit**
- Each run start, finish and cancel is logged on the viewer's stderr with repository, mode, provider/model and child PID.

## 4. Delivery plan (small, separate PRs)

1. **Backend**: job manager, child-process runner, token and Origin middleware, the `/api/*` routes, input validation. No UI.
2. **UI**: `/run` form and live log page in vanilla JS and Go templates, following the existing `static/` and `templates/` style (no build step, embedded assets).
3. **Docs**: viewer doc page in all four locales, and the README feature list synced to the translations.
4. *(Follow-up, if wanted)*: `ocr scan` from the UI, reusing the same runner.

Testing: `httptest` coverage for every security check (token, cookie, Origin, Content-Type, body size, path and ref validation, loopback refusal), and the job manager tested against a fake child process (the `TestHelperProcess` pattern) for streaming, reconnect replay, cancellation and timeouts. The 90% coverage threshold holds.

## 5. Open questions for maintainers

1. Is an opt-in flag on `ocr viewer` the right shape, or would you prefer a separate subcommand?
2. Is a child process acceptable, or would you rather make `internal/stdout` per-run so reviews can run in-process?
3. Repository path: free input (optionally limited by `--allow-run-root`), or only repositories that already have sessions under `~/.opencodereview/sessions/`?
4. Should `ocr scan` be part of the first round?


### Alternatives Considered

- **A separate wrapper project** that starts the CLI. This loses the integration with the existing session pages and repeats all of the security work outside the project.
- **Running reviews in-process.** This is blocked by the global `internal/stdout` writer and the process-wide signal handling, and a panic in one review would stop the viewer.
- **WebSocket instead of SSE.** A two-way channel is not needed. SSE is simpler, reconnects on its own and needs no dependency.


### Affected Area

WebUI Viewer, CLI / Commands

### Additional Context

_No response_
issues.triage_reason: Large multi-PR feature in internal/viewer (job manager, child-process runner, auth token/CSRF middleware, SSE, UI) with explicit open design questions for maintainers; docs part would touch pages/, which is off limits.
issues.skip_reason: coder gave up: Issue #1582 is a design proposal with unresolved open questions for maintainers (flag vs subcommand, child process vs in-process, repo path policy, scan scope) and a multi-PR plan including docs under pages/, which is disallowed. No change made pending maintainer decision.
issues.repro_notes: Feature request (opt-in run feature for ocr viewer), not a bug. Any test would fail only because new code is missing (compile error), so no regression test was added.

issues.title: Multi-Agent CI: Parallel PRs, Cross-PR Conflict Detection, Agent Context
issues.body:
## Description

Open Code Review is exactly what I need for my multi-agent AI workflow. Running multiple Claude Code agents in parallel means lots of generated code, and having deterministic + model-assisted review before merge is critical.

## Use Case

Setup:
- Multiple AI agents generating code on separate Git worktrees
- Each agent's output needs automated review before PR creation
- Security scanning for injection, XSS, secrets

## Question: Multi-Agent CI Integration

I'm trying to set up Open Code Review in a workflow where:
1. Agent A creates a PR from worktree-A
2. Agent B creates a PR from worktree-B
3. Both PRs trigger Open Code Review via GitHub Actions

### Questions:
1. **Parallel execution** — Can Open Code Review run on multiple PRs simultaneously without state conflicts?
2. **Cross-PR awareness** — If Agent A and Agent B both modify the same file, can Open Code Review flag this as a potential conflict even though they're in separate PRs?
3. **Agent-attributed findings** — Can findings be tagged with which agent generated the code? This helps with auditability in multi-agent setups.

### Feature Request: Agent Context

It would be valuable to pass agent metadata (agent ID, branch name, worktree path) to Open Code Review so findings can be correlated back to specific agents.

## Security Config

For sensitive repos, can Open Code Review run entirely locally without sending diffs to external models? The docs mention model access — is there an air-gapped mode?

Excellent project — this is the missing piece for safe multi-agent development.
issues.triage_reason: The issue is mostly questions plus several vague, large feature requests (cross-PR conflict detection, agent attribution metadata, air-gapped mode). It has no concrete, small, checkable change and needs maintainer design decisions.

issues.title: feat(review): --delta-from to review only files changed since a previous session
issues.body:
### Problem Statement

When a change under review gets a new version (feedback addressed, a rebase, one more commit), OCR re-reviews every file, including the ones the new version didn't touch.

`--resume` almost handles this. It reuses per-file checkpoints keyed on a fingerprint of each file's own diff (`reviewItemFingerprint`). But `ValidateResume` rejects the whole run as soon as `source_artifact_sha256` differs, which is by design: resume means "finish the same input". So there is no supported way to say "this is the next version of that change; only review what's different."

On a multi-file change where a new version touches one or two files, that means paying for the full review again. It's also part of what #1206 describes: small follow-up changes taking as long as the original review.

### Proposed Solution

Add an opt-in flag:

```bash
ocr review --from main --to feature --delta-from <session-id>
```

It would behave like `--resume` with the whole-input identity check removed:

- A file is reused only when its per-file diff is byte-identical to the parent's, so its comments and line numbers apply exactly as recorded. Changed, new and deleted files are dispatched as usual.
- Everything else `--resume` checks still applies: range or commit mode only, same repository, same rule config and file filter, and no implicit provider or model change.
- The mixing concern in `resume_identity.go` ("a report in which no field distinguishes the two") is covered by making the delta visible:
  - `parent_run_id` names the earlier session.
  - Reused files are listed under `coverage.reused`.
  - `"delta": true` goes on the `resume_lineage` record and in the JSON `resume` block.
  - `ocr session show` prints `Parent: run <id> (delta)`.
- It can't be combined with `--resume` or `--preview`.
- Documented limit: a reused file isn't reviewed again, so a finding in an unchanged file that depends on code in a changed file isn't re-checked.

I have a working implementation with tests and docs (in all five locales), about 350 lines, most of it tests and docs. I can open the PR if this direction works for you.

### Alternatives Considered

- **Hunk-level delta:** re-review only the changed hunks and move earlier findings to their new line numbers. It saves more, but needs finding identity and fix verification across versions. That's a much larger design, so it's better as a follow-up.
- **Loosening `--resume` itself:** this would change the meaning of an existing flag and lose the strict "same input" guarantee that current users rely on.
- **Scripting it outside OCR** (diff the two versions and pass `--exclude` for unchanged files): this drops the earlier findings from the output, so the report for the new version is incomplete.

### Affected Area

CLI / Commands, Review Agent / LLM interaction, Output / Formatting

### Additional Context

**Data from a production pipeline.** We run an internal multi-model review pipeline on every uploaded revision, and OCR runs as one of its reviewers. In September we moved updated revisions from a full re-review to a delta review. Per-review usage from that system's records, Aug 25 – Sep 16, completed reviews only:

| Review | n | median tokens | median cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| First upload (full) | 262 | 1.17M | $1.46 |
| Update, full re-review (before delta reviews existed) | 125 | 2.23M | $2.53 |
| Update, delta review | 32 | 248k | $0.42 |

That covers two repositories reviewed by separate lanes, 32 delta reviews across 25 revisions. The saving holds in each lane on its own: 1.76M → 122k tokens ($2.11 → $0.27) in one, and 3.17M → 336k tokens ($3.11 → $0.42) in the other.

Updates cost more than first uploads because a revision that needs a new version tends to be the larger, harder one, and each re-upload paid for the whole change again. A delta review cut the median update by 89% in tokens and 83% in dollars.

Caveats:

- Delta reviews have only been running since Sep 9, so n = 32 is still small.
- Full updates that ran after that date (38, median $3.18) are fallbacks, skewed toward larger changes, so the table compares against the period before instead.
- That pipeline's delta works at the patch level (the hunk-level alternative above). The file-level version proposed here will save less, in proportion to how many files a new version leaves untouched.
- Dollar figures exclude subscription-billed roles.

issues.title: [RFC] Machine-enforceable issue claiming workflow (/accept, /assign)
issues.body:
### Problem Statement

Issue ownership today is informal: contributors express interest in comments, and maintainers assign by hand. That works when volume is low and responses are fast, but ownership is easy to lose track of as the project grows — especially around good first issues and other community-facing work.

A small, machine-enforceable claiming protocol would make ownership explicit for both contributors and maintainers, without turning this into a project-management system.

### Proposed Solution

Add one GitHub Actions workflow that reacts to issue comments with three commands:

| Command | Who | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/accept` | maintainers (write / maintain / admin) | mark the issue ready for public claiming (`accepted`) |
| `/assign` | any contributor | claim the issue if it is open, claimable, and currently unassigned |
| `/unassign` | current assignee or a maintainer | release the issue |

**Claimable** means the issue is open and any of:

- labeled `accepted`, or
- already labeled `good first issue`, or
- already labeled `help wanted`

Hard rules:

- first valid `/assign` wins; never overwrite an existing assignee
- the bot never revokes a manual maintainer assignment
- closed issues ignore all commands
- unknown commands are no-ops
- repeated `/assign` from the same person is idempotent

### Why this shape

The goal is only:

1. maintainers decide acceptance
2. contributors decide whether to claim
3. the bot enforces ownership

Out of scope for a first iteration: prow-style command suites, workgroup taxonomies, title-format checks, PR admission gates, and any change to existing issue templates or CI.

### Alternatives Considered

- Keep the current comment-based process: lowest cost, but ownership stays implicit.
- A full community lifecycle bot: more powerful, but heavier than this repo needs right now.
- This proposal: the smallest set of rules that makes claim state visible in GitHub.

### Labels

Two new labels only: `accepted`, `in-progress`. Existing labels are unchanged. Type labels from issue forms continue to work as they do today.

### Implementation shape (if this direction is wanted)

- one workflow file, e.g. `.github/workflows/issue-claim.yml`
- `actions/github-script` only (no new Python stack, no third-party bot)
- `permissions: issues: write, contents: read`
- estimated size: ~150–200 lines

### Questions for maintainers

1. Should `good first issue` / `help wanted` be claimable without `/accept`?
2. Who may run `/accept` — write / maintain / admin only?
3. Any concern about slash commands versus free-form comments?
4. Is a tracking issue + small PR welcome, or is the current manual process preferred for now?

Happy to follow up with a focused PR if the direction looks right.
issues.triage_reason: The RFC's only deliverable is a new .github/workflows/issue-claim.yml, a path the bot may not edit, and it still has open maintainer questions on policy and direction.
issues.skip_reason: triage: not feasible: The RFC's only deliverable is a new .github/workflows/issue-claim.yml, a path the bot may not edit, and it still has open maintainer questions on policy and direction.

issues.title: token budget not enforced
issues.body:
### OpenCodeReview Version

open-code-review v1.12.1 (5589990) linux/amd64 built at: 2026-09-15T21:56:40+08:00

### Operating System

Linux (x86_64)

### Installation Method

Built from source

### LLM Provider

Other OpenAI-compatible endpoint

### Bug Description

Supplementary write-up for #1247. --max-tokens-budget is only checked
inside dispatchSubtasks, right before starting the *next* group
(agent.go ~685-698), and that's the only place the budgetExceeded flag
gets set:

    if a.args.MaxTokensBudget > 0 {
        ...
        if projected > a.args.MaxTokensBudget {
            ...
            a.budgetExceeded.Store(true)
        }
    }

The only place that flag is read is inside a group's own round loop
(agent.go:1449):

    if round > 1 && a.args.MaxTokensBudget > 0 && a.budgetExceeded.Load() {
        ...
        break
    }

With the default --concurrency 8, a diff producing 8 or fewer groups
dispatches all of them in the first pass, so there's never a "next
group" to trigger the check, budgetExceeded never flips true, and no
other code path polls real aggregate usage mid-run.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Read internal/agent/agent.go ~685-698 (the only site that sets
   budgetExceeded) and :1449 (the only site that reads it).
2. Confirm there is no other call site for budgetExceeded.Store(true) and
   no per-round live-usage check outside this flag — grep for
   "MaxTokensBudget" and "budgetExceeded" across internal/agent/*.go.
3. Confirm main has no StopTokenBudget symbol (the fix PR #1248
   introduces this; it isn't merged).
4. Cross-reference against #1247's live repro: 4-file diff,
   --max-tokens-budget 2000000, default --concurrency 8 → finished at
   12.15M tokens (~6x budget), all groups reported completed, no budget
   warning.

### Expected Behavior

Aggregate token usage should be checked before every round inside a
running group, not only when a next group is about to dispatch, so runs
that never dispatch a "next" group still respect --max-tokens-budget.

### Logs / Error Output

```shell
go build ./... / go vet ./... / go test ./... all clean at commit
5589990.
```

### AI/LLM Disclosure

- [ ] I didn't use AI/LLM to assist or generate the content above.

### Additional Context

Supplements #1247 (PR #1248 open, not yet merged, adds the missing
per-round check).
AI disclosure: this report was investigated and drafted with AI
assistance (Claude), verified against the source at commit 5589990 via
direct code reading plus go build/vet/test — not via a live LLM-driven
review run.
