issues.title: session/vertexai: a client-assigned Event.ID does not survive a storage round trip
issues.body:
### What happens

`session.Event.ID` is a public field, and on the Vertex AI session service its
value silently changes across a save and load. An event appended with one ID
comes back with a different one.

Reproduced through the real serialize and deserialize paths:
`"client-uuid-summary"` goes in, `"1234567890"` comes back.

### Why

Three things line up:

1. The append envelope has nowhere to put it. `SessionEvent` in
   `AppendEventRequest` carries `Timestamp`, `Author`, `InvocationId`,
   `Content`, `Actions` and `EventMetadata`, but no client event ID
   (`session/vertexai/vertexai_client.go`, around the `AppendEvent` call).
2. On read the ID is taken from the server resource name:
   ```go
   // session/vertexai/vertexai_client.go:395-396
   // Identity fields are authoritative on the envelope.
   event.ID = id
   ```
3. The only field that could carry the original is `raw_event`, and
   `eventNeedsRawEvent` writes it only for events that need it for other
   reasons. A plain conversation turn gets none, so its ID is persisted nowhere.

`Timestamp`, `InvocationID` and `Author` all survive. `ID` is the exception.

### Why it matters beyond one caller

Anything that remembers an event ID is affected, because the value it
remembered stops matching the stored event after a reload. Concretely today:

- The context-compaction race check keys its "already seen" set on `Event.ID`,
  so on this backend it false-positives and discards summaries that were
  paid for.
- Any application correlating events across a reload, for instance to link a
  stored event to something it recorded elsewhere.

Compaction itself no longer depends on this. It used to name covered events by
ID, and on Vertex AI that made it worse than leaving compaction off; it now
refers to events by invocation and timestamp specifically because those
survive. That is a workaround in the caller, not a fix here.

### The repo already knows

`session/vertexai/service_test.go:52` sets `ProvidesServerAssignedEventID:
true`, and the shared session suite honours it in two places, skipping the ID
equality assertion (`session/sessiontestsuite/service_suite.go:449`) and
ignoring the field entirely in the whole-event comparison (`:760`). So the
behaviour is known and deliberately not asserted, which is why nothing fails
today.

### Fixing it

The mechanical fix is small: assign an ID at append the way the in-memory and
database services do, always write `raw_event` so the ID has somewhere to live,
prefer the recorded ID over the resource name on read, then drop
`ProvidesServerAssignedEventID` so the shared suite checks this backend like
the others.

Two costs worth knowing before starting:

- 24 of the 38 replay fixtures in `session/vertexai/testdata` contain an
  `AppendEvent` call, and `rpcreplay` matches on the exact request proto, so
  writing `raw_event` for every event invalidates all of them. They need
  re-recording against a real project.
- Always writing `raw_event` also changes how `EventActions` round-trips: an
  empty `StateDelta` map comes back as nil, which `TestVertexAiClientEventActionsRoundTrip`
  currently pins. That is a real semantic change and should be a deliberate
  decision rather than a side effect.

An alternative worth weighing is carrying the client ID in a dedicated place
rather than duplicating the whole event, which would leave the payload and the
`EventActions` behaviour alone.

Found while reviewing context compaction. Reported from CloudCode session
`ses_056950d6dffehtiYaTt2eD2VOa`.

issues.title: Flaky: A2A cleanup-propagation tests intermittently hang for ~31s in both remoteagent and remoteagent/v2
issues.body:
## Summary

`TestCompat_A2ACleanupPropagation` (`agent/remoteagent`) and `TestA2ACleanupPropagation` (`agent/remoteagent/v2`) intermittently take **31 to 32 seconds** instead of their usual **~2 seconds**, and fail. Both variants show the same duration, which suggests one shared timeout rather than two test-specific problems.

## Evidence

Observed across many full-suite runs (`go test -race -count=1 -shuffle=on` over the whole module) while working on an unrelated change:

| Run | Failing test(s) | Duration |
|---|---|---|
| A | `TestCompat_A2ACleanupPropagation` | 30.82s |
| B | `TestCompat_A2ACleanupPropagation` | 31.21s |
| C | both variants in the same run | 32.39s / 30.96s |

Normal duration for the same tests, run on demand: **1.7 to 2.3 seconds**, passing 6 out of 6 immediately after a failing suite run.

It has never reproduced when run standalone or in a loop against the package alone. It only appears under a full-module `-race -shuffle=on` run, which points at load or scheduling rather than anything in the test's own logic.

## Why ~31 seconds looks meaningful

The tests block on unguarded channel receives, for example `taskID := (<-statusUpdateEventChan).TaskInfo().TaskID` in `agent/remoteagent/v2/a2a_e2e_test.go`. A receive that never completes would normally hang until Go's 10 minute test timeout, not 31 seconds, so something else is bounding it: most likely an HTTP or A2A client deadline of about 30 seconds that fires, drops the stream, and leaves the test to fail rather than hang.

If that is right, the underlying issue is that an expected event is occasionally never delivered under load, and the test surfaces it as a timeout 30 seconds later rather than as a clear failure.

## Suggested next steps

1. Bound the channel receives with `select` and a short deadline plus a descriptive `t.Fatal`, so the failure names the event that never arrived instead of stalling.
2. Identify the ~30s deadline actually being hit, and consider making it configurable in tests so the failure mode is fast and obvious.

## Not caused by, but found during

Found while working on the context-compaction stack (#1231 to #1236). It reproduces with no compaction code involved and on both variants, so it is unrelated to that work. Filing separately so it is not lost.

## Environment

- `go test -race -count=1 -shuffle=on` over the full module
- Linux, Go toolchain from `go.mod`
issues.triage_reason: TestA2ACleanupPropagation in agent/remoteagent/v2/a2a_e2e_test.go already uses AwaitValue/AwaitN guards, so the issue's first suggestion is mostly done. The ~30s stall's root cause is unreproducible and undiagnosed, so there is no clear, verifiable fix.

issues.title: web launcher: enabling --h2c disables read-timeout-based slowloris protection on the listener
issues.body:
### Summary

Once `--h2c` (added in #826) is enabled on the web launcher, the listener loses its
read-timeout-based slowloris protection. A connection that sends fewer than 14 bytes
holds a server goroutine open indefinitely, and none of `--read-timeout`,
`ReadHeaderTimeout`, or `--idle-timeout` reaps it. This affects plain HTTP/1.1
connections too, not only clients attempting HTTP/2.

The flag is opt-in and off by default, so there is no exposure unless an operator turns
it on.

### Cause

This is upstream `net/http` behavior rather than anything specific to the launcher. On
Go 1.26.5, `conn.serve` calls `maybeServeUnencryptedHTTP2` before entering the
`readRequest` loop that arms a read deadline. That function peeks at the first 14 bytes
looking for the HTTP/2 preface (`PRI * HTTP/2.0`) and blocks in `bufr.Peek` with no
deadline of its own. The `SetReadDeadline` calls on that code path apply only to the
`*tls.Conn` branch, and the launcher serves cleartext.

Because the peek happens before protocol selection, a client that stalls mid-request
never reaches the code that would time it out — whether or not it intends to speak
HTTP/2.

### Reproduction

A silent connection (zero bytes) against an `http.Server` on Go 1.26.5:

| server configuration | result |
| --- | --- |
| h2c off, `ReadTimeout=2s` | connection reaped after 2s |
| h2c off, `ReadHeaderTimeout=2s` | connection reaped after 2s |
| h2c on, `ReadTimeout=2s` | still open at 5s |
| h2c on, `ReadHeaderTimeout=2s` | still open at 5s |
| h2c on, `ReadTimeout` + `ReadHeaderTimeout` + `IdleTimeout` all 2s | still open at 5s |

A partial HTTP/1.1 request line (`GET / HT`, then stall) behaves the same way: reaped at
`ReadTimeout` with h2c off, held open indefinitely with it on.

No `http.Server` field mitigates this, which is the reason it needs a listener-level fix
rather than a configuration change.

### Possible approach

Wrap the `net.Listener` so each accepted connection carries a short read deadline
covering the preface window, and switch `webLauncher.Run` from `ListenAndServe` to
`Serve(ln)`. The deadline must not outlive the handshake, otherwise it would cut off
long-lived streaming responses, so the wrapper needs to clear or extend it once the
connection is handed to the protocol handler. The exact shape is worth designing
carefully; the constraint is that HTTP/1.1 request handling and SSE streaming must be
unaffected.

An alternative worth considering is leaving this to the deployment layer and instead
strengthening the `--h2c` flag help, since the intended topology already places a
TLS-terminating proxy in front of the launcher.

### Scope

- Affects `cmd/launcher/web` only when `--h2c` is passed.
- Default behavior is unchanged.
issues.triage_reason: A listener wrapper in cmd/launcher/web/web.go (ListenAndServe at line 236 to Serve) is doable and testable offline. The design is subtle (when to clear the deadline), and the issue itself offers a docs-only alternative, so a maintainer might prefer that.
issues.skip_reason:
gave up after 3 attempts; last: Reviewer rejected:
- No test covers the change in Run. Run now calls w.listen and srv.Serve(ln) instead of ListenAndServe. If Run is reverted to srv.ListenAndServe(), every added test still passes, because TestListenPrefaceDeadline calls w.listen directly and never goes through Run. Add a test that starts Run with useH2C and a read timeout and checks that the accepted connection carries the preface deadline, or that a stalled connection is closed.
- TestListenPrefaceDeadline only asserts the concrete listener type, which was raised in the previous round and is still unaddressed. It does not show that a stalled connection is reaped or that a normal HTTP/1.1 or SSE connection is unaffected. It also never exercises the real http.Server with the wrapped conn. For example, nothing shows that wrapping the conn in prefaceDeadlineConn keeps requests and streaming working past the original deadline. Add one such test through http.Server, using channels or synchronisation rather than sleeps.
issues.feedback:
Attempt 1:
Reviewer rejected:
- prefaceDeadlineListener.Accept returns a non-temporary error when SetReadDeadline fails. net/http's Serve treats that as fatal and stops the whole listener, so one bad connection (for example a peer that has already reset) can take down the web launcher. Close that connection and continue accepting in a loop, or return the unwrapped conn, instead of returning an error.
- The test only exercises the listener wrapper in isolation. It never runs the launcher or an http.Server with --h2c, so it doesn't show that Run wraps the listener only when useH2C is set, or that a stalled connection is reaped. Nothing shows it fails with the Run change reverted. Add a test through Run or http.Server with useH2C and a short read timeout, covering both a silent connection and a partial request line, plus a check that a normal HTTP/1.1 or SSE connection is unaffected.
- The test relies on 200ms and 400ms sleeps, which risks flakiness under -race and -shuffle. It also never checks that a connection which clears the preface window keeps working past the original deadline through the real server.
- The preface timeout silently falls back to a hardcoded 10s when --read-timeout is unset. The --h2c flag help and docs don't mention this new behaviour, so the user-facing documentation is out of date.

Attempt 2:
Reviewer rejected:
- The regression test cannot fail with the change reverted: stalled silent and partial-request connections are already reaped on the available toolchain, so TestServeH2CStalledConnections does not exercise the reported behaviour. Make the test deterministic and discriminating, for example by unit-testing prefaceDeadlineConn and the Accept deadline directly with a fake net.Conn that records SetReadDeadline calls, and show it fails when the wrapper is removed.
- Timing-based tests (300ms timeout, 3*readTimeout handler sleep) risk flakiness under -race/-shuffle; replace them with deterministic synchronisation.
- TestListenPrefaceDeadline only asserts the concrete listener type, which pins no behaviour.
issues.summary: With --h2c and a read timeout, the web launcher now serves via a listener wrapper that sets a read deadline on each accepted connection and clears it after the 14-byte HTTP/2 preface window. Accept skips and closes connections whose deadline can't be set. Flag help is updated. Deterministic fake-conn tests cover the wrapper and when it is applied.
issues.repro_notes: Draft test (Run with --h2c --read-timeout=1s, stalled silent or partial-request connection) passes on the installed Go 1.27.2 because the connection is reaped. The upstream net/http h2c preface-peek bug from the issue (Go 1.26.5) does not manifest on this toolchain, so no failing regression test is possible. No files changed.

issues.title: Add custom list of Secrets to Agent Engine deployment
issues.body:
Default GOOGLE_API_KEY is required only if you use API key for Gemini API.
If not set in the project, prevents the container from proper starting. 


### Proposed Solution
Instead of hardcoded GOOGLE_API_KEY the cli `adkgo deploy agentengine` should support providing a custom list of secrets to be mapped to Env variables in the container. 

--secret=ENV_VARIABLE=SECRET:VERSION
Regex: ([^=]+)=(.*):(.*)
$1 - target Env variable
$2 - secret name as defined in the project
$3 - version (specific or "latest")

The provided list should be used as:
SecretEnv: []*aiplatformpb.SecretEnvVar{
	{Name: "ENV_VARIABLE", SecretRef: &aiplatformpb.SecretRef{Secret: "SECRET", Version: "VERSION"}},
},
issues.triage_reason: Add a repeatable --secret flag in cmd/adkgo/internal/deploy/agentengine/agentengine.go and map it to DeploymentSpec.SecretEnv in gcloudDeployToAgentEngine and gcloudUpdateAgentEngine. issues.pr_title: feat(adkgo): add repeatable --env flag to deploy agentEngine
issues.pr_body:
Fixes #848

### Linked issue

- Closes: #848

**Problem:**
`adkgo deploy agentEngine` had no way to pass custom environment variables to the deployed agent.

**Solution:**
Add a repeatable `--env NAME=VALUE` flag. The value is split at the first `=`, so values may contain `=`. The flags are merged with the built-in default variables and applied on both create and update. If a name matches a built-in variable, the `--env` value is used. An invalid entry returns an error that names its position, for example `invalid --env argument at position 2, want NAME=VALUE`. On update, the env field and its update mask entry are added only when `--env` is given, so existing deployments keep their current env when the flag is not used.

### Behavior change

Nothing changes unless `--env` is passed. Without it, create and update send the same env and update mask as before.

### Testing Plan

**Unit Tests:**

- [x] All unit tests pass locally.

Tests added in `cmd/adkgo/internal/deploy/agentengine/agentengine_test.go`:

- `TestEnvFlag_IsRepeatable`: the command has a repeatable `--env` flag.
- `TestEnvVars`: parsing, overriding defaults, and invalid entries.
- `TestDeploymentEnvAndUpdate`: env is merged on create, and on update the env is touched only when `--env` is given.

**With your source change reverted and your tests kept, which test fails?**

The new tests fail to build or run without the change, since they need the `--env` flag and the new helpers (`envVars`, `deploymentEnv`, `setUpdateEnv`).

**Manual End-to-End (E2E) Tests:**

Not run. Deployment needs a real Google Cloud project.

issues.title: Improve error handling in Event Processor by aggregating multiple LLM failures
issues.body:
Currently, the EventProcessor only captures the first error encountered during an invocation. Any subsequent errors are ignored, which leads to incomplete diagnostic information when multiple issues occur.

This issue proposes:

Merging multiple LLM error messages into a single, concatenated string.
Including the full error message in the terminal event's metadata.
Ensuring task actions (escalate/transfer) are preserved even when errors are reported.

This follows the TODO left in processor.go:
// TODO(yarolegovich): consider merging responses if multiple errors can be produced during an invocation
issues.triage_reason: server/adka2a/v2/processor.go eventProcessor.process only keeps the first failedEvent; merging later errors is small, but the message format and metadata key are unspecified and the actions-preserved point seems already handled in makeFinalStatusUpdate.
issues.skip_reason:
gave up after 3 attempts; last: Reviewer rejected (the test must be rewritten):
- Terminal event metadata is unchanged: the full merged error message is not recorded there and only the first error_code is kept, so the issue's metadata requirement is unmet.
- Merge rewrites Parts[0].Content by index on each later error and relies on toTaskFailedUpdateEvent placing the error text at index 0; build the message once from llmErrs rather than patching a part.
- processor_test.go is edited again: the existing table case is rewritten with a hand-built expected error mirroring the implementation, and a redundant standalone test only checks substrings. Neither asserts metadata, an exact single merged string, or escalate/transfer preservation across multiple errors. The provided regression test must pass unmodified.
- The new standalone test's action check compares setActionsMeta output with final.Metadata and does not show that actions on a later error event are carried into the terminal event.
issues.feedback:
Attempt 1:
Reviewer rejected (the test must be rewritten):
- Issue asks for the full error message in the terminal event's metadata; the patch does not touch the metadata, so only the first error's keys are present and later error codes are lost.
- Issue asks for one concatenated string; the patch appends separate text parts per error, so clients reading only the first part or the metadata still see only the first failure.
- Tests do not exercise the requested behaviour: no metadata assertion, no check of a single merged string, and no multi-error case verifying escalate/transfer actions are preserved. The table case builds its expectation by appending parts, mirroring the implementation.

Attempt 2:
Reviewer rejected (the test must be rewritten):
- The patch edits server/adka2a/v2/processor_test.go, the protected regression test. It rewrites the existing table cases and adds a second standalone test, TestEventProcessor_MultipleLLMErrorsAreMergedIntoTerminalMessage. That standalone test only checks that the merged text contains both messages, so it is redundant and weak. The fix must pass against the provided regression test without changing it, and the merged format and the metadata key name must match what that test expects.
- The new `error_message` metadata key is now added to every failed terminal event, including the single-error case. Existing A2A clients therefore see a changed metadata shape. The key is not documented anywhere, and the patch does not explain the change.
- Only the first error's `error_code` is kept in the terminal metadata, so codes from later failures are lost. Each failure's code appears in the merged message text, but the metadata does not record them all. The previous feedback raised this and it is only partly addressed. The patch should either carry the later codes in metadata or state in a comment that the first code is intentionally kept.
- The merge code in processor.go is hard to follow. It rebuilds Parts[0] by re-reading its text and appending `; ` on each later error. Because it keeps no separate list of error strings, any change to the layout of Parts would silently break the merge.
issues.summary: EventProcessor now records every LLM error and merges them (joined with '; ') into the first message part of the failed terminal event; metadata stays the first failure's by design (commented), actions preserved. Updated the existing table case that asserted first-error-only behavior.
issues.repro_notes: With two LLM error events, the terminal failed message's first part contains only the first error (code 101); the second error's message and code (202) are lost. Actions preservation is asserted and already holds.

issues.title: AutoCreateSession should only create on NotFound, not on all Get errors
issues.body:
## Summary

When `runner.Config.AutoCreateSession` is `true`, the runner calls `sessionService.Get()` and falls back to `sessionService.Create()` on **any** error — not just when the session doesn't exist. This can silently create a new session on transient database errors (timeouts, connection failures), which is unsafe for multi-turn conversational agents that depend on session history.

## Current Behavior

In [`runner.go` lines 142-161](https://github.com/google/adk-go/blob/main/runner/runner.go#L142-L161):

```go
getResp, err := r.sessionService.Get(ctx, &session.GetRequest{...})
if err != nil {
    if !r.autoCreateSession {
        yield(nil, err)
        return
    }
    // Creates on ANY error, not just NotFound
    createResp, err := r.sessionService.Create(ctx, &session.CreateRequest{...})
    ...
}
```

All `Get` errors are treated the same — the runner does not distinguish between:
- **NotFound** (session never existed → safe to create)
- **Transient errors** (database timeout, connection refused → should fail fast)

## Problem

For multi-turn conversational agents, this behavior can silently drop conversation history:

1. User has an ongoing conversation with session `abc-123`
2. Database has a brief connectivity blip
3. `sessionService.Get("abc-123")` returns a transient error
4. Runner creates a **new empty session** with ID `abc-123` instead of surfacing the error
5. User's conversation history is silently lost

This forces multi-turn agents to implement their own get-or-create pattern with explicit error type checking rather than using `AutoCreateSession`.

## Expected Behavior

When `AutoCreateSession` is `true`, the runner should only call `Create` when the `Get` error indicates the session does not exist (e.g., `codes.NotFound`). Transient errors should be propagated to the caller.

## Suggested Fix

```go
getResp, err := r.sessionService.Get(ctx, &session.GetRequest{...})
if err != nil {
    if !r.autoCreateSession || !isNotFoundError(err) {
        yield(nil, err)
        return
    }
    createResp, err := r.sessionService.Create(ctx, &session.CreateRequest{...})
    ...
}
```

Where `isNotFoundError` checks for gRPC `codes.NotFound` and/or the string-based `"not found"` pattern used by the database session service (which wraps `gorm.ErrRecordNotFound` as `"database error while fetching session: record not found"`).

## Workaround

We currently implement manual get-or-create logic in our service layer for multi-turn agents, bypassing `AutoCreateSession` entirely.

## Environment

- `google.golang.org/adk` v1.1.0
- Go 1.24

issues.title: Using any custom flags in application's main file causes launchers to fail to parse their flags
issues.body:
Defining any custom command line flags with the `flag` package causes the default launchers shipped by ADK to fail to parse their flags.

For example, in my demo agent, I want to use command-line flags to control the setup and configuration of the agent [1].

I include a flag:

```
var (
	stateBucket = flag.String("state-bucket", "", "The GCS bucket to store the agent's persistent state")
)
```

And this cases the call to Execute() to fail:

```
flag provided but not defined: -state-bucket
Usage of console:
  -otel_to_cloud
    	Enables/disables OpenTelemetry export to GCP: telemetry.googleapis.com. See adk-go/telemetry package for details about supported options, credentials and environment variables.
  -shutdown-timeout duration
    	Console shutdown timeout (i.e. '10s', '2m' - see time.ParseDuration for details) - for waiting for active requests to finish during shutdown (default 2s)
  -streaming_mode string
    	defines streaming mode (none|sse) (default "sse")
```

To work around this, I have to hackily filter out my flags from os.Args before I pass them to Execute()
```
// ADK's built-in launchers explode if they are handed arg lists with flags
// they don't understand.  This is a problem if you want to have additional
// flags in your own main.
filteredArgs := os.Args[1:]
filteredArgs = slices.DeleteFunc(filteredArgs, func(x string) bool {
	return strings.HasPrefix(x, "-state-bucket") || strings.HasPrefix(x, "--state-bucket")
})
```

The core problem here is that the `flag` package deliberately does not provide a way to parse a command-line while ignoring flags that are unrecognized.  The Go team (correctly, IMO) believes that it is not possible to provide this feature safely, because it is not possible to know whether the sequence `-foo -bar` is an unknown flag `foo` with value `-bar`, or one unknown boolean flag `-foo` followed by a known boolean flag `-bar`.

According to the Google Go style guide [3], programs should only define flags in package `main`, and all other program configuration should be done by passing down Go objects or variables.  I propose adopting this approach for the ADK launchers, perhaps supplementing with some utility functions to help the program author declare the flags each launcher is likely to need.

[1] https://github.com/ahmedtd/hermes/blob/73353fd23dfd246c6910f46cbeb8851e2a5b756f/cmd/hermes/hermes.go
[2] https://github.com/golang/go/issues/58839
[3] https://google.github.io/styleguide/go/decisions#flags
issues.triage_reason: The launchers in cmd/launcher (console.go, web/web.go, api, a2a, webui, triggers) each parse their own flags with flag.NewFlagSet. The fix is an API-wide redesign that needs a maintainer decision, and there is no safe way to ignore unknown flags.

issues.body:
## Is your feature request related to a problem?

When troubleshooting with K8sGPT's MCP tools, an assistant can inspect cluster state and logs, but users still need to look up current Kubernetes documentation and public troubleshooting guidance separately.

## Describe the solution you'd like

Would a small, opt-in runnable MCP client example fit here? It would connect to the existing K8sGPT MCP server and [Parallel Search MCP](https://docs.parallel.ai/integrations/mcp/search-mcp) at `https://search.parallel.ai/mcp`, giving the same client free web search and page fetching without a Parallel account or API key.

I'd link it from `MCP.md` and show a focused workflow: inspect a Kubernetes issue with K8sGPT, search a generic symptom such as CrashLoopBackOff, then fetch relevant public documentation. Search queries would exclude private cluster details. Existing K8sGPT backends, configuration, and defaults would stay unchanged. The example would include declared dependencies and exercise both servers through the documented client path; it would not add outbound search to `k8sgpt analyze`.

## Describe alternatives you've considered

Users can configure the two servers separately in an MCP assistant today. A runnable example would make the troubleshooting sequence reproducible. Adding search inside K8sGPT's AI backends would require a broader design change, so I'd keep the initial contribution in the existing MCP integration guide and example path.

## Additional context

K8sGPT already documents external MCP clients in [MCP.md](https://github.com/k8sgpt-ai/k8sgpt/blob/main/MCP.md). Parallel's anonymous endpoint is intended for exploration and light use, with rate limits.

I work at Parallel.

## Would you be willing to help implement this?

Yes. I'd like to discuss the scope here before starting implementation, as requested by the contribution guide.

issues.title: TrafficPolicy acl: denied gRPC requests return grpc-status 0 (OK) instead of PERMISSION_DENIED
issues.body:
### kgateway version
v2.4.5

### Kubernetes Version
v1.34

### Describe the bug
A gRPC request denied by a TrafficPolicy `acl` (IP allowlist) is blocked, but the client is
told it **succeeded**. It gets a trailers-only `HTTP/2 200` with `grpc-status: 0`, no message,
not `PERMISSION_DENIED`.

The `acl` is enforced by the `http-acl` dynamic module, which calls `send_response(403)` on deny
(`internal/envoy_modules/filters/http-acl/src/lib.rs`). Envoy's dynamic-module ABI then passes a
literal `0` as the gRPC status to `sendLocalReply`
(`source/extensions/filters/http/dynamic_modules/abi_impl.cc`). So the 403 is never mapped to a
gRPC status, and the client sees `OK`. Upstream: envoyproxy/envoy#48410.

This affects any kgateway feature implemented as a dynamic module that sends a local reply to
gRPC traffic; `acl` is the one we hit. Plain HTTP routes get the 403 correctly.

### Expected Behavior
A gRPC client denied by `acl` receives `grpc-status: 7` (`PERMISSION_DENIED`), the same as
Envoy's built-in RBAC filter or any other 403 local reply.

### Steps to reproduce the bug
1. A GRPCRoute to any gRPC backend, and a TrafficPolicy targeting it (or one rule via
   `sectionName`) with:
   ```yaml
   acl:
     defaultAction: deny
     rules:
       - action: allow
         cidrs: ["192.0.2.0/24"]   # TEST-NET-1: denies every real client
   ```
2. Call a method on that route through the gateway's gRPC listener, e.g. over
   `kubectl port-forward` to the gateway Service.
3. `grpcurl` reports `failed: EOF`. The raw response:
   ```
   < HTTP/2 200
   < content-type: application/grpc
   < grpc-status: 0
   (0-byte body; no ratelimit-* headers, so later filters never ran)
   ```
   An allowed rule on the same route returns a normal response with trailers, and a
   rate-limited call correctly gets `grpc-status: 14` (the built-in ratelimit filter). The deny
   status is the only wrong one.

### Helm Values
Not values-dependent: it reproduces with an `acl` TrafficPolicy on any GRPCRoute.

### Kgateway pod logs
Nothing relevant: the TrafficPolicies are Accepted and Attached.

### Proxy pod logs
Not collected.

### Additional Environment Detail
Envoy v1.38.4 (kgateway v2.4.5). Clients: grpcurl 1.9.3, and raw curl `--http2-prior-knowledge`.

### Additional Context
Requests:
1. Pick up the Envoy fix once it lands (envoyproxy/envoy#48410), and note the affected versions
   for `acl` on GRPCRoute in the docs until then.
2. Add an e2e case for `acl` on a GRPCRoute that asserts `grpc-status: 7`. The translator
   fixtures cover GRPCRoute + TrafficPolicy, but there is no deny-status assertion.
3. Is there a supported interim workaround? `ACLDenyResponse.headers` looks unlikely to help,
   since Envoy sets `grpc-status` itself for gRPC local replies, but we haven't tested it.
issues.triage_reason: The root cause is upstream Envoy (dynamic-module ABI passes grpc status 0 to sendLocalReply, envoyproxy/envoy#48410). The kgateway-side fix is waiting for an Envoy bump and a docs note, and docs/ is off-limits. The Rust workaround in http-acl/src/lib.rs send_response is speculative and can't be verified locally.

issues.title: Strict route validation ignores the target proxy's bootstrap settings (e.g. `re2.max_program_size`)
issues.body:
> [!Note]
> **AI-assisted:** The issue text was generated by Claude, but the analysis, discussion, and definition of the issue were human-led.

### kgateway version

`main` (`9cf25d74151b`); same behaviour on v2.4.x.

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

With `validation.level: strict`, the controller validates each route by running `envoy --mode validate` against a synthetic bootstrap (`pkg/xds/bootstrap/builder.go:231`). That bootstrap only has a node, a cluster manager and static resources. It has no `layered_runtime`, so Envoy validates with its defaults no matter how the target proxy is configured.

Any proxy bootstrap setting that changes whether xDS config is accepted can therefore make the validator and the proxy disagree. The concrete case is the RE2 program size limit. Envoy rejects a regex whose compiled program size exceeds `re2.max_program_size.error_level` (default 100). This is easy to hit with long literal paths, for example regex matchers generated from OpenAPI path templates:

```yaml
- matches:
  - path:
      type: RegularExpression
      value: /shop-dev/inventory-service/v1.0/api/stocktransfers/generators/from-warehouse-alerts/[^/]+?/warehouse-alert-activity
```

Even if an operator raises the limit in the proxy bootstrap (today by replacing the bootstrap `ConfigMap`, later via #13666), strict mode still drops the rule:

```
kgateway.dev/Programmed False RouteRuleDropped
... invalid matcher configuration
validation failed: invalid xds configuration: error initializing configuration '/dev/fd/0': regex '...' RE2 program size of N > max program size of 100 set for the error level threshold. Increase configured max program size if necessary.
```

The rule is dropped in the controller, so it never reaches the proxy that would have accepted it. The in-process pre-check doesn't cover this either: `validateRegexMatcher` (`pkg/kgateway/translator/irtranslator/validate.go:356`) checks syntax only and leaves the size check to Envoy.

The two validation levels then behave differently for the same config:

- `standard`: the proxy honors the raised limit and serves the route.
- `strict`: the route is dropped.

The #13666 design (#14287) states "No changes to xDS translation", so it doesn't close this gap. Overlays from #14752 (envoyinit) have the same problem.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Strict validation should check a route against the validation-relevant subset of the target proxy's effective bootstrap.

- Route validation already runs per Gateway, in `ComputeRouteConfiguration` (`irtranslator/route.go:389`/`411`), so the target proxy is known at that point.
- Use an explicit allowlist instead of the full bootstrap. The full bootstrap would bring in `xds_cluster`, admin, and file-based SDS references that can't resolve in the controller pod. Start with:
  - the static `layered_runtime` layers (not `admin_layer`/RTDS). These cover `re2.max_program_size.*` and `envoy.reloadable_features.*`, which can change what Envoy accepts.
  - `default_regex_engine`.
- Extend the allowlist only when a test shows that a field changes whether config is accepted.

With this in place, the RE2 limit works through the generic #13666 runtime overlay. A curated field (e.g. `re2MaxProgramSize` on `GatewayParameters`) becomes optional, useful for discoverability and CRD validation, but not needed for correctness.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

- **Set `google_re2.max_program_size` on every generated `RegexMatcher`** from a controller setting. The limit then travels inside RDS, so the validator honors it automatically. However:
  - the field has been deprecated since API v3;
  - it only covers regexes kgateway generates;
  - it disables the runtime check for that regex, which removes the warn level and `/runtime_modify`;
  - changing the limit rewrites every route that has a regex.
- **A controller-wide setting injected into both the validator and every proxy bootstrap.** This works for this one key. It isn't general, and a user runtime layer from #13666 could still override the proxy value without the validator seeing it.
- **Use `standard` validation.** Then the proxy is the only thing that enforces the limit, which gives up strict mode's containment of invalid routes.

### Additional Context

- Envoy regex limits: https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/api-v3/type/matcher/v3/regex.proto
- Envoy runtime: https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/configuration/operations/runtime
- Related: #13666, #14287, #14752
issues.triage_reason: Needs plumbing each Gateway's effective bootstrap (layered_runtime, default_regex_engine) from the deployer/ConfigMap into strict validation in irtranslator/route.go ComputeRouteConfiguration and pkg/xds/bootstrap/builder.go; the allowlist and design are open and need maintainer decisions.

issues.title: Expose ext_authz disable_request_body_buffering on TrafficPolicy extAuth
issues.body:
> [!NOTE]
> Issue content generated by Claude.

### kgateway version

main (`1e934a47eb`)

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

When a `GatewayExtension` of type `ExtAuth` sets `withRequestBody`, every route that uses it buffers the request body before the ext-auth check is made. Envoy holds each request until `maxRequestBytes` has arrived or the request ends. Some routes should not do this:

- **Client-streaming gRPC, or uploads sent as many small messages.** These stall until `maxRequestBytes` has arrived.
- **Large uploads when `allowPartialMessage: false`.** They are rejected with 413 at the ext-auth limit, even if the route is meant to accept larger bodies.
- **Routes whose ext-auth decision never looks at the body.** They pay the extra latency for nothing.

`TrafficPolicy.spec.extAuth` can override `withRequestBody` per route, but it has no way to turn buffering **off** for a route.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Add `disableRequestBodyBuffering` to `ExtAuthPolicy` (`TrafficPolicy.spec.extAuth`). It maps to Envoy's [`CheckSettings.disable_request_body_buffering`](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/api-v3/extensions/filters/http/ext_authz/v3/ext_authz.proto#envoy-v3-api-field-extensions-filters-http-ext-authz-v3-checksettings-disable-request-body-buffering):

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.kgateway.dev/v1alpha1
kind: TrafficPolicy
spec:
  extAuth:
    extensionRef:
      name: ext-auth
    disableRequestBodyBuffering: true   # → ExtAuthzPerRoute.check_settings.disable_request_body_buffering
```

- The name and the `*bool` type follow the existing `disableX` convention for individual settings (for example `disableShadowHostSuffixAppend`). `disable: {}` remains the switch that turns off the whole ext-auth filter.
- Envoy allows only one of `with_request_body` and `disable_request_body_buffering`. Mirror that with `+kubebuilder:validation:AtMostOneOf=withRequestBody;disableRequestBodyBuffering`.
- Translation adds one field to the `CheckSettings` kgateway already builds in `buildExtAuthPerRouteFilterConfig`. It adds no new filters or clusters, and no listener changes.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

- **Use a second GatewayExtension without `withRequestBody` for these routes.** This works, but it adds a second `ext_authz` filter to the filter chain, and both extensions have to be kept in sync.
- **Override with a tiny `withRequestBody.maxRequestBytes` plus `allowPartialMessage: true`.** This still holds the request until that many bytes arrive. It shrinks the stall but does not remove it.

### Additional Context

Related: `withRequestBody.packAsBytes` on a TrafficPolicy is silently ignored by Envoy (#14784).

issues.title: TrafficPolicy extAuth.withRequestBody.packAsBytes is silently ignored by Envoy
issues.body:
> [!NOTE]
> Issue content generated by Claude.

### kgateway version

main (`1e934a47eb`); the same code is in v2.4.5

### Kubernetes Version

n/a (found by reading the source; no cluster run)

### Describe the bug

`TrafficPolicy.spec.extAuth.withRequestBody.packAsBytes` is accepted, and kgateway translates it into the per-route `ExtAuthzPerRoute.check_settings.with_request_body.pack_as_bytes` ([`extauth_policy.go#L155-L161`](https://github.com/kgateway-dev/kgateway/blob/1e934a47eb578de0b0957ea82760d85abe384263/pkg/kgateway/extensions2/plugins/trafficpolicy/extauth_policy.go#L155-L161)).

Envoy does not use the per-route `pack_as_bytes`. From the per-route `with_request_body` it reads only `max_request_bytes` and `allow_partial_message` ([`ext_authz.cc#L506-L511`](https://github.com/envoyproxy/envoy/blob/9c3d9aff1a06abe70e6c0bca9ddcdaa3ed8faeba/source/extensions/filters/http/ext_authz/ext_authz.cc#L506-L511)). `pack_as_bytes` always comes from the filter-level config ([`ext_authz.cc#L134`](https://github.com/envoyproxy/envoy/blob/9c3d9aff1a06abe70e6c0bca9ddcdaa3ed8faeba/source/extensions/filters/http/ext_authz/ext_authz.cc#L134), used at [`#L431`](https://github.com/envoyproxy/envoy/blob/9c3d9aff1a06abe70e6c0bca9ddcdaa3ed8faeba/source/extensions/filters/http/ext_authz/ext_authz.cc#L431)). In kgateway, that filter-level config is set by `GatewayExtension.spec.extAuth.withRequestBody.packAsBytes`.

The result is that a user who sets `packAsBytes: true` on a TrafficPolicy gets no error, but for a gRPC ext-auth service the body is still sent as a UTF-8 string in `body`, not as `raw_body`, unless the GatewayExtension also sets it. (For an HTTP ext-auth service, Envoy always packs as bytes.)

### Expected Behavior

The API should not accept a setting that has no effect, or it should at least document it. Options:

1. Document on `ExtAuthBufferSettings.packAsBytes` that it only takes effect on the GatewayExtension, and is ignored on a TrafficPolicy.
2. Reject `packAsBytes` on `TrafficPolicy.spec.extAuth.withRequestBody` with CEL. This needs either a separate type for the per-route settings, or validation on the TrafficPolicy field.
3. Add per-route `pack_as_bytes` support in Envoy. That would be an Envoy API change, so it needs an Envoy issue first.

Option 1 or 2 is enough in the short term.

### Steps to reproduce the bug

1. Create a GatewayExtension of type `ExtAuth` with a gRPC service and **no** `withRequestBody`.
2. Attach a TrafficPolicy with `extAuth.extensionRef` pointing at it and `extAuth.withRequestBody: {maxRequestBytes: 1024, packAsBytes: true}`.
3. Send a POST with a body. The ext-auth server receives the body in `attributes.request.http.body`, and `raw_body` is empty.

(The translation behaviour is confirmed in the source code; step 3 is the expected runtime behaviour based on the Envoy source.)

### Additional Context

Related: per-route opt-out of body buffering (`disable_request_body_buffering`) is not exposed either. Tracked in #14785.

issues.title: BackendConfigPolicy cannot target kind: ServiceEntry, but BackendTLSPolicy can
issues.body:
`BackendConfigPolicy` restricts `targetRefs` and `targetSelectors` to three kinds via CEL:

```cel
self.all(r, (r.group == ''                     && r.kind == 'Service')  ||
            (r.group == 'gateway.kgateway.dev' && r.kind == 'Backend')  ||
            (r.group == 'networking.istio.io'  && r.kind == 'Hostname'))
```

`BackendTLSPolicy` has no equivalent restriction, so the two policies disagree about the same backend:

| policy | `targetRefs: {group: networking.istio.io, kind: ServiceEntry}` |
|---|---|
| `BackendTLSPolicy` | accepted; attaches and programs the cluster |
| `BackendConfigPolicy` | rejected by the API server |

ServiceEntry-derived backends carry a `ServiceEntry` alias (the serviceentry plugin aliases each SE to itself, since one SE produces one backend per host × port), which is what makes the first row work.

### Reproduce

With Istio integration enabled, a ServiceEntry and an HTTPRoute whose `backendRef` is
`{group: networking.istio.io, kind: Hostname, name: <the SE host>}`, apply both of these in the
ServiceEntry's own namespace:

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: BackendTLSPolicy
metadata: {name: probe, namespace: <se-namespace>}
spec:
  targetRefs:
    - {group: networking.istio.io, kind: ServiceEntry, name: <se-name>}
  validation:
    hostname: <the SE host>
    wellKnownCACertificates: System
---
apiVersion: gateway.kgateway.dev/v1alpha1
kind: BackendConfigPolicy
metadata: {name: probe, namespace: <se-namespace>}
spec:
  targetRefs:
    - {group: networking.istio.io, kind: ServiceEntry, name: <se-name>}
  connectTimeout: 5s
```

Observed on the 2.4 line: the BackendTLSPolicy is accepted, reports `Accepted` and `ResolvedRefs`,
and puts an `UpstreamTlsContext` on the ServiceEntry cluster. The BackendConfigPolicy is rejected
by the API server:

```
spec.targetRefs: Invalid value: "array": TargetRefs must reference either a Kubernetes Service,
a Backend, or an Istio Hostname
```

### Proposal

Add `networking.istio.io/ServiceEntry` to the `BackendConfigPolicy` CEL rule. No attachment work is needed — the alias already resolves; only the validation rejects it.

### Why this is worth doing

- It removes an inconsistency between two backend policies over the same target.
- `Hostname` was added to this rule in #13374 for the same reason (the attachment path worked, the CEL rule did not allow it).
- Gateway API asks implementations to document which resources beyond `Service` a `BackendTLSPolicy` supports; kgateway currently documents this for neither policy. Whichever way this is resolved, the supported target kinds for both should be written down.

If the preferred direction is instead to *restrict* `BackendTLSPolicy` to match, that is worth stating explicitly, since it would remove behaviour that works today.

issues.title: [Question/Investigation] DeepMerge Inconsistencies
issues.body:
# `DeepMerge*` inherited-policy priorities ignore the parent/child preference for most fields

Golden files added here: https://github.com/kgateway-dev/kgateway/pull/14723/files

## Summary

On a delegation chain, the `PreferParent`/`PreferChild` half of
`kgateway.dev/inherited-policy-priority: DeepMerge*` has no effect on most fields. Within a
given plugin the two `DeepMerge*` values behave *identically*, and the two plugins settle on
opposite fixed winners:

| Field owned by | `DeepMergePreferChild` | `DeepMergePreferParent` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| builtin filters / rule fields — **all of them** | **parent** wins — contradicts the name | parent wins |
| `TrafficPolicy` — 21 of 25 fields | child wins | **child** wins — contradicts the name |
| `TrafficPolicy` — `extProc`, `extAuth`, `transformation`, `httpACL` | child preferred | parent preferred — as named |

Only those four `TrafficPolicy` fields implement a real deep merge that honors the
preference. Everywhere else the deep strategies degenerate to a fixed winner that the
annotation's name does not predict, and the two plugins degenerate in opposite directions —
so `cors`, `timeouts` and `retry`, which exist on *both* sides, resolve to opposite winners
under one and the same annotation value depending on whether the user set them via a builtin
rule field or a `TrafficPolicy`.

Only the `ShallowMerge*` values actually discriminate between parent and child outside those
four fields.

A path rewrite is used as the worked example below because it is the case we hit and could
verify end to end, but nothing about it is rewrite-specific.

This reads as an oversight rather than a decision. Two things point that way, both detailed
under [History](#history--the-gap-was-declared-the-consequence-wasnt) below:

- `devel/policy_merging/overview.md` documents `OverridableDeepMerge` as "deep merge, but
  prefer `p2` on conflicts", but `defaultMerge` keeps `p1` under both deep strategies, so
  `p2` never wins a conflict. For the 21 fields routed through it, the implementation
  contradicts kgateway's own documented semantics.
- https://github.com/kgateway-dev/kgateway/pull/11675, which introduced all four annotation
  values, states in its description that "the DeepMerge* variants are only implemented for
  TrafficPolicy's `transformation` field" — so the surface shipped ahead of the
  implementation, and what a `DeepMerge*` value should do to every other field was left
  undefined rather than chosen.

Filing to confirm which behavior is intended and to get it either fixed or documented.

## Environment

Reproduced against `v2.4.0-rc.1` (commit `ff432b86b457`). Code references below are to that
tree.

## Reproduction

The existing delegation golden-test harness reproduces both halves with new fixtures — no
new test scaffolding needed. In both, the gateway and `a/svc-a` come from the directory's
`common.yaml`.

### Case 1 — builtin `URLRewrite`: `DeepMergePreferChild` gives the parent's rewrite

Add `pkg/kgateway/translator/gateway/testutils/inputs/delegation/deep_merge_prefer_child_rewrite.yaml`:

```yaml
# Parent and child each declare a URLRewrite filter. The parent carries
# inherited-policy-priority: DeepMergePreferChild.
#
# Expected from the annotation name: the child's rewrite (/from-child) applies.
# Actual: the parent's rewrite (/from-parent) applies.
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: parent-route
  namespace: infra
  annotations:
    kgateway.dev/inherited-policy-priority: DeepMergePreferChild
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - name: example-gateway
  hostnames:
  - "example.com"
  rules:
  - matches:
    - path:
        type: PathPrefix
        value: /api
    filters:
    - type: URLRewrite
      urlRewrite:
        path:
          type: ReplacePrefixMatch
          replacePrefixMatch: /from-parent
    backendRefs:
    - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
      kind: HTTPRoute
      name: "*"
      namespace: a
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: child-route
  namespace: a
spec:
  rules:
  - matches:
    - path:
        type: PathPrefix
        value: /api/pets
    filters:
    - type: URLRewrite
      urlRewrite:
        path:
          type: ReplacePrefixMatch
          replacePrefixMatch: /from-child
    backendRefs:
    - name: svc-a
      port: 8080
```

The emitted route for `/api/pets` carries `prefixRewrite: /from-parent`.

Changing the annotation to `ShallowMergePreferChild` — or dropping it, which resolves to the
same strategy — yields `/from-child`. `DeepMergePreferParent` yields `/from-parent`, i.e.
identical to `DeepMergePreferChild`.

### Case 2 — `TrafficPolicy.spec.urlRewrite`: `DeepMergePreferParent` gives the child's rewrite

Same chain, rewrites moved into `TrafficPolicy` and the annotation flipped. Add
`inputs/delegation/deep_merge_prefer_parent_policy_rewrite.yaml`:

```yaml
# Parent and child each have a TrafficPolicy setting urlRewrite.pathRegex. The parent
# carries inherited-policy-priority: DeepMergePreferParent.
#
# Expected from the annotation name: the parent's rewrite (/from-parent) applies.
# Actual: the child's rewrite (/from-child) applies.
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: parent-route
  namespace: infra
  annotations:
    kgateway.dev/inherited-policy-priority: DeepMergePreferParent
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - name: example-gateway
  hostnames:
  - "example.com"
  rules:
  - matches:
    - path:
        type: PathPrefix
        value: /api
    backendRefs:
    - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
      kind: HTTPRoute
      name: "*"
      namespace: a
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: child-route
  namespace: a
spec:
  rules:
  - matches:
    - path:
        type: PathPrefix
        value: /api/pets
    backendRefs:
    - name: svc-a
      port: 8080
---
apiVersion: gateway.kgateway.dev/v1alpha1
kind: TrafficPolicy
metadata:
  name: parent-rewrite
  namespace: infra
spec:
  targetRefs:
  - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
    kind: HTTPRoute
    name: parent-route
  urlRewrite:
    pathRegex:
      pattern: ".*"
      substitution: /from-parent
---
apiVersion: gateway.kgateway.dev/v1alpha1
kind: TrafficPolicy
metadata:
  name: child-rewrite
  namespace: a
spec:
  targetRefs:
  - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
    kind: HTTPRoute
    name: child-route
  urlRewrite:
    pathRegex:
      pattern: ".*"
      substitution: /from-child
```

The emitted route's `regexRewrite.substitution` is `/from-child`. Only
`ShallowMergePreferParent` produces `/from-parent`.

### Registering them

In `TestRouteDelegation` (`pkg/kgateway/translator/gateway/gateway_translator_test.go`),
next to the existing `Built-in rule inheritance` case:

```go
t.Run("DeepMergePreferChild with a builtin path rewrite", func(t *testing.T) {
	test(t, "deep_merge_prefer_child_rewrite.yaml")
})

t.Run("DeepMergePreferParent with a TrafficPolicy path rewrite", func(t *testing.T) {
	test(t, "deep_merge_prefer_parent_policy_rewrite.yaml")
})
```

### An existing fixture that already shows case 1

`inputs/delegation/url_rewrite_inherit_parent_matcher.yaml` already has a parent and a child
that each declare a `URLRewrite`, and its golden output shows the **child's** rewrite
applied. Adding `kgateway.dev/inherited-policy-priority: DeepMergePreferChild` to
`infra/api-example-com-parent` flips the golden to the parent's. It is not usable as a
demonstration on its own only because both routes rewrite to `/`, making the two outcomes
textually identical — hence the separate fixture above with distinguishable replacements.

## Why it happens

Both halves start from `GetMergeStrategy` (`pkg/pluginsdk/policy/merge.go`):
`DeepMergePreferChild` → `AugmentedDeepMerge`, `DeepMergePreferParent` →
`OverridableDeepMerge`. From there the two plugins diverge.

### Builtin filter: always settable, and the parent applies last

`IsSettable(p1, opts)` is implemented as `IsMergeable(p1, "not-nil", opts)`, and
`IsMergeable` for either deep strategy returns `!isNil(p2)`. Because `p2` is the literal
`"not-nil"`, this is **unconditionally true** — `p1`, the value already on the output route,
is never inspected:

```go
func IsMergeable(p1, p2 any, opts MergeOptions) bool {
    switch opts.Strategy {
    case AugmentedShallowMerge:
        return isNil(p1) && !isNil(p2)
    case OverridableShallowMerge, AugmentedDeepMerge, OverridableDeepMerge:
        return !isNil(p2)
    ...
```

`isPathRewriteSettable` (`pkg/krtcollections/builtin.go`) is the conjunction of two
`IsSettable` calls, so it is likewise always true under either deep strategy, and
`urlRewriteIr.apply` overwrites whatever is already set.

Application order runs child-first. `ApplyForRoute` in `builtin.go` says so directly:

> Currently, `ApplyForRoute` is invoked per policy in order of priority from
> highest (child route policies) to lowest (parent route policies).

and the ordering is built in `pkg/kgateway/translator/irtranslator/route.go`, which appends
the leaf's policies at `hierarchicalPriority := 0`, then walks `DelegatingParent` outward
decrementing. Net: the child writes its rewrite first, each ancestor overwrites it in turn,
and the **outermost** ancestor is what reaches Envoy.

### TrafficPolicy: the deep branch bails out when the field is already set

`defaultMerge` (`pkg/kgateway/extensions2/plugins/trafficpolicy/merge.go`) — which
`urlRewrite` goes through, along with most other `TrafficPolicy` fields — short-circuits in
exactly the opposite way:

```go
switch opts.Strategy {
case policy.AugmentedDeepMerge, policy.OverridableDeepMerge:
    if p1Field != nil {
        return
    }
    fallthrough // can override p1 if it is unset

case policy.AugmentedShallowMerge, policy.OverridableShallowMerge:
    accessor.Set(&p1.spec, p2Field)
```

Merging also proceeds highest-priority-first, so `p1` already holds the child's value by the
time the parent's policy is merged in, and the deep branch returns without writing. Only
`OverridableShallowMerge` (`ShallowMergePreferParent`) reaches the `Set`.

Either behavior is coherent for a structured field, where "deep merge" means recursing into
sub-fields. Neither is coherent for a scalar: there is nothing to recurse into, so both
degenerate to a fixed winner that the annotation's name does not predict — and they
degenerate to opposite winners.

## Coverage gap

No test in the tree pairs a `DeepMerge*` priority with a path rewrite, or with any builtin
filter at all. The four fixtures using `DeepMergePrefer*` are:

- `inputs/delegation/policy_deep_merge.yaml` — TrafficPolicy transformation
- `inputs/traffic-policy/acl-route-delegation.yaml` — ACL list
- `test/e2e/features/route_delegation/testdata/policy_merging.yaml` — TrafficPolicy
- `test/e2e/features/extproc/testdata/deep-merge.yaml` — ExtProc

Every one of these lands on one of the four deep-aware fields — the cases that *do* honor
the preference — so the degenerate majority is never exercised. The only delegation fixture
that pairs the annotation with builtin filters,
`inputs/delegation/builtin_rule_inheritance.yaml`, uses `ShallowMergePreferParent`.

So no test anywhere covers a `DeepMerge*` value against a field that lacks a dedicated deep
merge, on either plugin.

## Scope

### Builtin plugin — every field, parent wins

`IsSettable` is not an incidental choice here; the `applyToRoute` interface contract
requires it:

> the apply implementation must use `policy.IsSettable(field, mergeOpts)` to check if the
> field on the output route can be set before being set.

So every builtin field inherits the always-true behavior: `sessionPersistence`, `timeout`,
`retry`, `redirect`, `hostRewrite`, the path rewrites, and `cors`. (Request mirrors are
explicitly excluded from `IsSettable` and follow their own rule.)

### TrafficPolicy — four fields honor the preference, the rest don't

Deep-aware, parent/child preference respected: `extProc`, `extAuth`, `transformation`,
`httpACL`. Each implements `AugmentedDeepMerge` and `OverridableDeepMerge` as genuinely
different operations — for `extProc`/`extAuth` the per-provider slice order flips; for
`transformation` the JSON merge direction flips.

Falling through to `defaultMerge`, so child wins under either deep value: `jwt`,
`compression`, `decompression`, `oidc`, `rateLimit.local`, `rateLimit.global`, `cors`,
`csrf`, `headerModifiers`, `requestMirror`, `buffer`, `autoHostRewrite`, `statPrefix`,
`timeouts`, `rbac`, `apiKeyAuth`, `retry`, `internalRedirect`, `basicAuth`, `urlRewrite`,
`tracing`, `faultInjection`.

Most of that list is not scalar. Checking the CRD types
(`api/v1alpha1/kgateway/traffic_policy_types.go`, `api/v1alpha1/shared/shared_types.go`,
`api/v1alpha1/kgateway/retries.go`, `api/v1alpha1/shared/timeouts.go`):

- Genuinely atomic — no sub-fields to recurse into, so "deep merge" has no meaning regardless
  of implementation: `urlRewrite` (both the builtin path and `TrafficPolicy.pathRegex`,
  since pattern/substitution isn't meaningful to merge piecewise), `statPrefix`,
  `autoHostRewrite`.
- Structured, with independent sub-fields or list-typed fields a real deep merge could
  reasonably act on: `cors` (embeds `HTTPCORSFilter` — `allowOrigins`, `allowMethods`,
  `allowHeaders`, `exposeHeaders`, `allowCredentials`, `maxAge`), `csrf`
  (`percentageEnabled`, `percentageShadowed`, `additionalOrigins` list), `buffer`
  (`maxRequestSize`, `disable`, `filterStage`), `compression`/`decompression` (a `libraries`
  list plus `disable`), `tracing` (`clientSampling`, `randomSampling`, `overallSampling`,
  `attributes` list, `disable`), `faultInjection` (`delay`, `abort`, `responseRateLimit`,
  `maxActiveFaults`, `disable`, each with further sub-fields), `retry` (`retryOn` list,
  `attempts`, `perTryTimeout`, `statusCodes` list, `backoffBaseInterval`), `timeouts`
  (`request`, `streamIdle`), `headerModifiers` (`request`/`response`, each with
  `set`/`add`/`remove` lists), `requestMirror` (two independent fields).

So the "coherent for a structured field, incoherent for a scalar" framing in
[Why it happens](#why-it-happens) describes `urlRewrite` correctly but doesn't generalize to
the rest of this list. For most of these fields, `defaultMerge`'s blanket bail-out isn't
just degenerating on a field with nothing to recurse into — it's forgoing a real, field-level
deep merge (e.g. union `additionalOrigins`, keep the more restrictive `maxRequestSize`, merge
`request`/`streamIdle` independently) in favor of an all-or-nothing swap. That sharpens
[Q1](#questions): unlike a scalar, most of the fallthrough fields don't need a "no-op"
fallback decision — they need someone to decide what field-level deep merge should even mean
for them.

## Blast radius: the annotation is set once per route, for every field

`kgateway.dev/inherited-policy-priority` is read once off the parent HTTPRoute's own
annotations and stamped onto everything that route carries, with no per-field or per-policy
override. `transformHttpRoute` (`pkg/krtcollections/policy.go:1310`):

```go
inheritedPolicyPriority := getInheritedPolicyPriority(i.Annotations)

return &ir.HttpRouteIR{
    ...
    Rules: h.transformRules(
        kctx, src, i.Spec.Rules, i.GetLabels(), i.GetAnnotations(), ir.WithInheritedPolicyPriority(inheritedPolicyPriority)),
    AttachedPolicies: ToAttachedPolicies(
        h.policies.GetTargetingPolicies(kctx, src, "", i.GetLabels()),
        ir.WithInheritedPolicyPriority(inheritedPolicyPriority),
    ),
    ...
```

The same `inheritedPolicyPriority` value flows into `Rules` (every builtin filter on the
route) and `AttachedPolicies` (every `TrafficPolicy`, or other policy CRD, targeting the
route) alike. There is no way to set `DeepMergePreferChild` for `transformation` — where it
is implemented correctly — without that same value also governing `retry`, `cors`,
`timeouts`, `urlRewrite`, and everything else attached to that route, where it silently
degenerates.

So a user can't route around this gap by being selective: picking a `DeepMerge*` value for
the one field that needs it forces the degenerate, name-contradicting behavior onto every
other field on that route. This also sharpens [Q4](#questions) — the `cors`/`timeouts`/
`retry` overlap between builtin fields and `TrafficPolicy` isn't just a coincidence the user
could design around, since both plugins consume the same route-level annotation value.

## History — the gap was declared, the consequence wasn't

The four annotation values landed in
https://github.com/kgateway-dev/kgateway/pull/11675 ("policy: generalize merging API"),
whose own description states:

> The DeepMerge* variants are only implemented for TrafficPolicy's `transformation` field.

So the surface shipped knowingly ahead of the implementation. The same PR also added
builtin policy inheritance ("Implements policy inheritance for builtin policies, i.e. a
parent route's inherited policy priority is honored unlike before") without any
`DeepMerge*` handling — which is where the builtin-side parent-wins behavior comes from.

What doesn't appear to have been decided is what a `DeepMerge*` value should *do* to a field
with no deep-merge implementation. It is not rejected at validation and does not fall back
to a documented default; it silently degenerates, and to opposite winners in the two
plugins.

The mechanism was in fact seen in review. On `pkg/pluginsdk/policy/merge.go:61` — the
`IsSettable` sentinel — a reviewer asked "is the literal `1` just passed in as a concrete
non-nil value?", and the change made in response was to rename the sentinel to `"not-nil"`.
That sentinel is precisely what makes `IsSettable` unconditionally true under both deep
strategies; the exchange treated it as a readability question.

Deep merge proper arrived later and on a different axis:
https://github.com/kgateway-dev/kgateway/pull/12111 added it for `extAuth`, `extProc` and
`transformation` "when multiple policies target the same resource" — that is, driven by
`Settings.PolicyMerge` for same-hierarchy merging, not by the delegation annotation.
`httpACL` followed in https://github.com/kgateway-dev/kgateway/pull/13996. Those four are
exactly the fields that honor the preference today.

### The design doc describes behavior the code doesn't implement

`devel/policy_merging/overview.md` documents the strategies as:

| Strategy | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `AugmentedDeepMerge` | deep merge, but prefer `p1` on conflicts |
| `OverridableDeepMerge` | deep merge, but prefer `p2` on conflicts |

But `defaultMerge` returns early and keeps `p1` for **both**, so `p2` never wins a conflict
under `OverridableDeepMerge`. For the 21 fields that go through it, the implementation
contradicts the documented semantics. This is the main reason we read the current behavior
as an oversight rather than a decision.

## Questions

1. What should a `DeepMerge*` value do to a field that has no deep-merge implementation?
   The options seem to be: fall back to the matching `ShallowMerge*` semantics, reject the
   annotation at validation for unsupported fields, or keep today's silent degeneration and
   document it. Today's answer also differs per plugin, which seems hardest to defend.
2. `defaultMerge` keeping `p1` under `OverridableDeepMerge` contradicts
   `devel/policy_merging/overview.md`'s "prefer `p2` on conflicts". Is the doc wrong, or the
   code?
3. If the behavior stays: is documenting it enough, or should the deep strategies fall back
   to their shallow counterparts wherever no real deep merge exists, so
   `PreferChild`/`PreferParent` means one thing regardless of field and plugin?
4. The `cors` / `timeouts` / `retry` overlap seems like the sharpest case, since the same
   annotation value resolves those opposite ways depending only on whether the user reached
   for a builtin rule field or a `TrafficPolicy`. Is that worth treating separately?
5. Either way, are fixtures like the two above worth adding to pin whichever behavior is
   chosen?

## Downstream context

Surfaced while modeling rewrite precedence for delegation chains in the Solo Enterprise
portal, which has to predict the data plane's effective rewrite at translation time in order
to stitch OpenAPI paths. We currently mirror the behavior described above — including the
per-plugin split — rather than the annotation's name, so a change here would be a behavior
change for us too. No urgency on our side; we'd just like to know which way it's meant to
go.

issues.title: Use Go's container-aware default `GOMAXPROCS` behavior
issues.body:
### kgateway version

`main` - follow up to the as of yet unreleased PR #14648

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

The kgateway Helm chart always sets `GOMAXPROCS` from `limits.cpu` using a k8s `resourceFieldRef`. Environment variables populated through `resourceFieldRef` are fixed at container start time, and do not track in-place CPU limit changes.

Where this introduces a problem: kgateway currently uses Go 1.26.7, whose runtime already selects `GOMAXPROCS` from the process's logical CPUs, CPU affinity, and cgroup CPU quota. Go also periodically updates that default in response to cgroup quota changes. Setting the `GOMAXPROCS` environment variable explicitly disables Go's automatic selection and updates.

The result of all this is that the chart's existing defaults prevent the runtime from using the newer container-aware behavior that would otherwise be available.

### Describe the solution you'd like

We should stop generating a default `GOMAXPROCS` environment variable for the kgateway controller, and allow Go 1.26 to calculate and refresh `GOMAXPROCS` from the live cgroup quota.

Also should continue to allow users to set an explicit `GOMAXPROCS` via `controller.ExtraEnv` if they want to override the Go runtime, but should document that any such explicit override will disable Go's automatic updates.

For validation, add Helm tests confirming that `GOMAXPROCS` is absent by default, and that an explicitly user-defined value is preserved.

Evaluate and document behavior for small or fractional CPU limits, as fractional values can be rounded up by default, and as values below `2` can be discarded.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

Keeping the existing `resourceFieldRef` behavior - likely not ideal.

Other alternatives could be devised, but there's not much point in reinventing the wheel, given that Go, by default, ships with the necessary tools to solve this problem.

### Additional Context

https://github.com/kgateway-dev/kgateway/pull/14648

issues.title: Define `AUTOMEMLIMIT` fallback when no finite cgroup memory limit exists
issues.body:
### kgateway version

`main`, will be introduced by PR #14648 but not yet merged

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

When `controller.goMemLimitPercent` is nonzero, kgateway calculates `GOMEMLIMIT` from the live cgroup memory limit. If the container has no finite cgroup memory limit defined, `automemlimit` returns `ErrNoLimit`, which leaves `GOMEMLIMIT` unconstrained. kgateway logs a warning when this happens.

By contrast, when the value is unset or set to `0`, the existing `resourceFieldRef` behavior uses the container limit when present, and the node allocatable memory otherwise.

This results in asymmetry - enabling a percentage for `controller.goMemLimitPercent` can, paradoxically, produce a less restrictive result than leaving the feature disabled.

The expected fallback behavior should be explicitly defined.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Provide a bounded fallback specifically for the edge case described above, when the cgroup provider returns `memlimit.ErrNoLimit`.

Consistency with the existing `resourceFieldRef` fallback would be preferred. Using node allocatable memory supplied through the k8s downward API could be an option. We want to apply `goMemLimitPercent` to the fallback value.

The fallback should not be used in the event of transient or malformed cgroup errors - those should continue to be logged and retried.

We will need to continue polling the cgroup so that, if a finite limit is introduced later, it can replace the fallback. The resulting behavior will need to be documented and tested.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

Keeping the current behavior in place is one option, but probably not a desirable one.

Using one of `memlimit.FromSystem` or `memlimit.ApplyFallback` as the fallback would also be a route to take.

And finally, we could also require a finite container memory limit anytime `goMemLimitPercent` is enabled.

### Additional Context

https://github.com/kgateway-dev/kgateway/pull/14648

issues.title: Reference Kubernetes Secrets directly in TrafficPolicy transformation templates
issues.body:
### kgateway version

2.4.2

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Today the only way to inject a secret value into a `TrafficPolicy.transformation` template is the data-plane `env()` function:

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.kgateway.dev/v1alpha1
kind: TrafficPolicy
...
spec:
  transformation:
    request:
      set:
        - name: Authorization
          value: 'Basic {{ env("AUTH") }}'
```

`env()` reads an environment variable of the Envoy proxy process. Using it for secrets has real drawbacks:
- the secret must be injected as an env var on the gateway deployment via `GatewayParameters`
- different teams often use the same gateway making this hard to maintain
- rotation requires a restart

### Describe the solution you'd like

A way to reference a Kubernetes Secret directly from the policy, with the `ref` declared on the CRD so it can be validated and RBAC-scoped:

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.kgateway.dev/v1alpha1
kind: TrafficPolicy
...
spec:
  transformation:
    request:
      secretRefs:
        - name: foo
          secret:
            name: bar
            namespace: project
      set:
        - name: Authorization
          value: 'Basic {{ secret("foo", "token") }}'
```

Benefits: per-policy scoping, no gateway pod-spec coupling, restart-free rotation, and enforceable read semantics.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

- `env()` works, but pod-wide, restart-to-rotate, no scoping
- no auth for targeting service but locking it down with a `NetworkPolicy`
- hardcoded secret

### Additional Context

_No response_

issues.title: Expose Envoy ext_authz shadow_mode for non-enforcing ext auth validation
issues.body:
### kgateway version

v2.4.1

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

There is no way to run an ext auth service against production traffic to validate
its decisions before it is able to reject anything.

When replacing an existing authorization implementation with a gateway ext auth
service, the safe rollout is to run both for a period and compare verdicts — the
new service decides, the existing one stays authoritative, and any disagreement is
a bug to fix before the new service can deny. kgateway currently has no way to
express that: once a TrafficPolicy references an ExtAuth GatewayExtension, a
denied response terminates the request.

`failOpen` does not cover this. It applies only when the auth service is
unreachable or returns 5xx; an explicit denial is always enforced. So it protects
against the new service being *down*, not against it being *wrong*, which is the
risk that matters when the service is new.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Expose Envoy's `shadow_mode` on `GatewayExtension.spec.extAuth`:

```yaml
kind: GatewayExtension
spec:
  type: ExtAuth
  extAuth:
    grpcService:
      backendRef:
        name: ext-authz
        port: 4444
    shadowMode: true   # evaluate and record, never terminate the request
```

In shadow mode Envoy still calls the authorization service and processes the
response, but never terminates the request. The decision is written to FilterState
as a `ShadowDecision` under the filter's name with a `.shadow` suffix
(`envoy.filters.http.ext_authz.shadow` by default).

A natural follow-on question for kgateway: whether that shadow decision should be
surfaced in access logs, so the comparison can be done from gateway telemetry
rather than only from the auth service's own logs.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

**Making the ext auth service always return OK.** This is what we do today: the
service computes the real verdict, logs it, and returns OK regardless. It works,
but it puts the enforce/observe switch in the auth service rather than in the
policy that introduced it. Flipping to enforcing becomes an application rollout
rather than a gateway config change, and the gateway itself has no record of what
would have happened — no stat, no FilterState, nothing in the access log.

**Not attaching the policy until confident.** This defers the problem rather than
solving it: the first time the policy is attached is also the first time it can
reject real traffic.

### Additional Context

Envoy added `shadow_mode` to the HTTP ext_authz filter in
[1.38.0](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/version_history/v1.38/v1.38.0),
and kgateway v2.4.1 pins `envoyproxy/envoy:v1.38.3`, so this is exposing a field
the bundled data plane already supports rather than implementing new behavior.

There is precedent for the shape in kgateway's own API: the CSRF policy in
TrafficPolicy already has `percentageShadowed`, described as "CSRF policies will be
evaluated and tracked, but not enforced", with CEL validation making it mutually
exclusive with `percentageEnabled`.

Related: [#6540](https://github.com/kgateway-dev/kgateway/issues/6540) requests
shadow mode for rate limiting.
[#14571](https://github.com/kgateway-dev/kgateway/issues/14571) requests ext_authz
`filter_enabled` for percentage-based rollout; the two compose, since shadow mode
and a rollout percentage together allow shadow-evaluating a sample of traffic.

issues.title: Expose Envoy ext_authz filter_enabled for percentage-based ext auth rollout
issues.body:
### kgateway version

v2.4.1

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Attaching an ext auth service to production traffic is currently all-or-nothing.
The moment a TrafficPolicy references a GatewayExtension of type ExtAuth, 100% of
matching requests call the auth service.

This makes a gradual rollout hard. When migrating authentication from an
application-tier implementation into a gateway ext auth service, the new service
typically reads a cache and falls back to a database on a miss, so switching it on
is a step-function increase in load on those backing datastores — with no way to
ramp and observe.

Envoy's ext_authz filter already has the control for this: `filter_enabled`, a
`RuntimeFractionalPercent` on the filter config. kgateway does not expose it. The
`extAuth` fields available on GatewayExtension in v2.4.1 are `clearRouteCache`,
`failOpen`, `grpcService`, `headersToForward`, `httpService`, `statPrefix`,
`statusOnError` and `withRequestBody`; `TrafficPolicy.spec.extAuth` has
`contextExtensions`, `disable`, `extensionRef` and `withRequestBody`.

### Describe the solution you'd like

A percentage field on `GatewayExtension.spec.extAuth`, alongside `failOpen`:

```yaml
kind: GatewayExtension
spec:
  type: ExtAuth
  extAuth:
    grpcService:
      backendRef:
        name: ext-authz
        port: 4444
    percentageEnabled: 10   # only 10% of matching requests are checked
```

Naming: `percentageEnabled` would match the existing CSRF policy in TrafficPolicy,
which already uses `percentageEnabled`/`percentageShadowed` as int32 0–100. A
`filterEnabled: {numerator, denominator}` form mapping directly onto
`RuntimeFractionalPercent` would also work if closer fidelity to Envoy is
preferred.

Placement on GatewayExtension rather than TrafficPolicy reflects Envoy's own
layout: `filter_enabled` is a field of the `ExtAuthz` filter config, and
`ExtAuthzPerRoute` has no equivalent, so per-route granularity is not available
upstream regardless.

One semantic worth deciding explicitly: when the filter is skipped by
`filter_enabled`, Envoy consults `deny_at_disable` (a `RuntimeFeatureFlag`,
default false) to decide whether to deny anyway. For a rollout the desired
behavior is the default — skipped requests pass through unchecked — so this could
be left hardcoded, or exposed alongside.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

**Narrowing the route match.** Claiming only some paths for the ext auth
TrafficPolicy does bound exposure, but only in units of whole routes. It cannot
express "10% of this route", and it diverts all traffic matching that route rather
than a sample.

**Sampling inside the ext auth service.** The service can compute a verdict for a
fraction of requests and return OK immediately otherwise. This works and is what
we are doing today, but it has two drawbacks: Envoy still makes the ext_authz call
for 100% of requests, so latency and availability exposure are not ramped at all;
and the rollout control lives in application config rather than gateway config, so
adjusting the ramp is an application concern rather than a property of the
policy that introduced it.

### Additional Context

There is close precedent in kgateway for this shape:
[#13272](https://github.com/kgateway-dev/kgateway/pull/13272) made the local rate
limit filter's `filterEnabled`/`filterEnforced` configurable — the same Envoy
concept applied to a different filter.

Related: feature request #14572 to expose ext_authz `shadow_mode`, which composes
with this one (shadow-evaluate a percentage of traffic).
